item.title: Photography at 200 through the Prix Pictet - 1854 Photography
item.description:
© Nadav Kander

As photography marks its bicentenary, the 11 Prix Pictet laureates demonstrate the different ways an image can draw us into the environmental and social questions shaping our world.

Two hundred years after Nicéphore Niépce fixed the view from his window, what can a photograph reveal beyond the scene in front of the camera? And what can photographers do to get our attention in an age when we are deluged by images alongside a continuous flow of fake news and misinformation? Can artists cut through all this to help us face the urgent challenge of climate catastrophe? Environmental destruction is extensively photographed, yet familiarity can dull our response. Does photography retain the power to bring about change, or to bring audiences into meaningful dialogue with the issues it depicts?

The 11 laureates of the Prix Pictet offer different approaches to these pressing questions. Founded by the Pictet Group in 2008 to draw attention to sustainability, the prize has recognised work encompassing documentary observation, constructed images, collaborative portraiture, thermal imaging and historical processes. Its successive themes, from ‘Water’ to ‘Storm’, connect environmental pressures with the societies that produce and experience them.

The inaugural winner, Canadian photographer Benoit Aquin, approached the issue of desertification in China through its effects on the people living with it. His winning series, The Chinese ‘Dust Bowl’, traces the consequences of intensive cultivation, overgrazing and depleted water supplies. Aquin’s photographs show people going about their lives amid dust storms caused by the loss of fertile soil. Carried by the wind, that soil becomes airborne pollution, spreading the consequences far beyond the region.

Nadav Kander’s Yangtze, The Long River (winner of the ‘Earth’ cycle) also considers the environmental and human costs of China’s rapid development. The London-based photographer shows people dwarfed by the infrastructure transforming the river landscape and displacing established communities. In Chongqing IV (Sunday Picnic), a gathering beneath a vast bridge gives these changes a human measure. The contrast raises a question running through the series: what is lost when economic progress depends on the destruction of communities and habitats?

Mitch Epstein (winner of the ‘Growth’ cycle) locates that relationship within his own country. His series American Power captures energy production among homes, roads and recreational spaces in the US, revealing how thoroughly its infrastructure shapes everyday experience. The title also directs us towards the political and corporate interests determining these landscapes. With writer Susan Bell, Epstein subsequently extended the project through billboards in Ohio and a website, taking its questions beyond the gallery.

Luc Delahaye, a former war reporter who turned to a more subjective approach, examines how power is exercised and whose lives it shapes. The French photographer’s winning portfolio (for the ‘Power’ cycle) brings political and economic gatherings into the same frame of inquiry as conflict and disaster. The large, detailed photographs invite sustained attention to the people within these events, connecting decisions made by political and business leaders with the unequal conditions in which others live. They extend the prize’s concern with sustainability to questions of authority, inequality and our responsibility towards one another.

Michael Schmidt’s Lebensmittel examines the industrial systems behind the food we eat. The German photographer documented farms, processing plants and packaged products, revealing stages of production usually hidden from consumers. Seen together, the images question the distance between food as a supermarket commodity and the animals, land and labour required to produce it.

Richard Mosse’s Heat Maps brings forced migration and the treatment of displaced people into the prize’s consideration of sustainability. The Irish artist used a military thermal camera to photograph refugee camps and temporary settlements, recording body heat rather than visible light. Designed for surveillance, the equipment renders people as anonymous heat signatures. His unsettling panoramas ask how societies accommodate those seeking refuge, and what happens when vulnerable people are treated as populations to monitor rather than individuals with rights and needs.

American photographer Sally Mann reaches into the medium’s past. Her Blackwater tintypes depict the Great Dismal Swamp, a refuge for people escaping slavery and a landscape subsequently scarred by extensive fires. The photographs’ dark, troubled surfaces suggest the difficulty of separating a place from the histories it holds. A 19th-century process becomes a way to consider the persistence of racial violence within the American South.

Ivorian artist Joana Choumali’s Ça va aller considers how people recover from collective trauma. Three weeks after the 2016 terrorist attack in Grand-Bassam, she used her iPhone to photograph subdued streets and solitary figures, then embroidered colourful thread directly onto the prints. The slow, repetitive stitching became a way to process her own grief and address feelings that often went unspoken. Awarded the prize under the theme of ‘Hope’, the series connects the wellbeing of a community with the difficult work of acknowledging suffering and finding ways to live with it.

Indian photographer Gauri Gill’s Notes from the Desert explores how marginalised communities sustain their lives in rural Rajasthan. Begun in 1999, the project records births, deaths, work and celebrations alongside the pressures of drought, poverty and limited access to healthcare and education. Through repeated visits and friendships, Gill shows how survival depends on relationships with one another and the natural environment. Awarded the prize under the theme of ‘Human’, the series places people often overlooked at the centre of questions about resources, inequality and collective wellbeing.

Valérie Belin approaches our relationship with resources through the things we acquire. The Frenchwoman’s Still Life compositions bring cheap, predominantly plastic consumer objects into the vanitas tradition, in which possessions become reminders of mortality. Their glossy abundance attracts the eye, while mannequin fragments suggest a human presence overwhelmed by accumulation. 

For Chilean-born artist, architect and filmmaker Alfredo Jaar, the response to the environmental crisis takes a more restrained form. The End depicts Utah’s Great Salt Lake, threatened by excessive water extraction. He chose to print the photographs at a modest size, describing them as a “visual whisper”. The scale requires an approach: viewers must move closer to encounter the immensity of what is being lost.

This month, The End and Belin’s Still Life will meet in conversation at Paris Photo, marking Pictet Group’s new official partnership with the fair. Their juxtaposition – exhibited together on the Promenoir at the heart of the Grand Palais – connects manufactured abundance with ecological depletion, using the familiar genres of still life and landscape to make us reconsider what beauty contains.

Neither attention nor understanding guarantees action. Across these 11 practices, however, photography creates occasions to question what we consume, how we live and whose experiences enter public view. Two centuries into its history, photography can still make familiar subjects newly visible, prompting us to reconsider what we thought we understood.

Prix Pictet presents Valérie Belin and Alfredo Jaar on the Promenoir at Paris Photo, Grand Palais, 12–15 November 2026, with a preview on 11 November.

item.title: Trading places: how the Print Swap app is helping photographers fill their walls with art - 1854 Photography
item.description:
St James’s Park © Simon Roberts.
All images available via Print Swap.

Sam Faulkner, the photographer behind Print Swap, discusses screen fatigue, status anxiety, and why the hardest part of swapping prints is getting people to ask

Sam Faulkner is a third-generation photographer – his father and grandfather were both professional photographers, though neither pushed him toward it. He found his own way in, straight out of university and off to Afghanistan, drawn to documentary work in the mould of Magnum Photos and Don McCullin. In 1995, the images he brought back won him the Ian Parry Award, and that grounding shaped Cocaine Wars, his long-term project on the cocaine trade across Colombia, Bolivia, Peru, Brazil, Haiti, Mexico and the US ( featured in British Journal of Photography, October 2007).

In 2001 Faulkner was commissioned by GQ to photograph Mario Testino, one of the world’s most glamorous image-makers, just ahead of Testino’s first-ever museum show at the National Portrait Gallery, London. From there came more work behind-the-scenes with Testino’s clients, such as brands Estée Lauder, Burberry and Michael Kors and then, as the editorial market thinned out, more commercial commissions. In the summer of 2015 Faulkner showed a five-year series of portraits at Somerset House, shot at Waterloo battlefield re-enactments, and published the book Unseen Waterloo: The Conflict Revisited. Portraiture and commercial work now pay the bills, but it is documentary photography that keeps the fire burning, as he puts it.

Faulkner is one of the UK’s most accomplished image-makers, but when it came to a blank patch on his own walls, he felt loath to hang up one of his own photographs. He also could not justify buying a print at gallery prices and, musing that “most photographers can’t afford that”, came up with an idea – Print Swap. Photographers exchange physical, editioned prints with each other. No money passes between them: each pays only for their own print to be produced and posted. Swaps are arranged through an iPhone app, no follower counts are visible, and the feed shows you the picture before it tells you who made it. Once both photographers have agreed a swap, professional labs around the world print both images on archival paper and ship them direct, each with a certificate of authenticity.

The thought of swapping evokes hit 1970s kids’ show, Multi-Coloured Swap Shop, but took Faulkner back to a conversation with Magnum photographer David Hurn, one of his mentors on the World Press Masterclass in the Netherlands back in 2001. Hurn said he had swapped prints with other image-makers throughout his career – ending up with more than 700 of them by the end. At the time Hurn’s words had not really registered. But, Faulkner now realised, if he had swapped just two prints a year since having that conversation, he would now own 50 prints by photographers he admired, and a house full of work instead of an empty wall.

“Hopefully there’s some sense of mutual appreciation. It’s always nice to have your work recognised by your peers – for them to look at it and think, that’s something I want to have around” – Sam Faulkner

The idea sat for a while. What tipped it into action was not a plan so much as a problem – twice over. First, a straightforward swap with a friend that ended up taking more than a year to complete, after Faulkner handed his print over at the pub and the friend showed up empty-handed. “Getting photographers to actually do the mechanics of the swap felt like a bit of friction,” he says. It was proof that even people who wanted to do this needed a system to make it happen. Then came a more general frustration, voiced one night in another bar with photographer friends “in various states of misery about the state of the business”. Nobody expected the economics of photography to improve for them any time soon, but this did mean they had capacity for other projects. “I’ve got a bit of time on my hands,” Faulkner remembers thinking. “Why don’t I give it a go?”

His case against simply buying or sharing images online is really a case against how little attention pictures get. “We’re surrounded by more images than we’ve ever seen,” he says. “How much attention do we give them when they’re 4cm x 4cm on your screen? You literally just swipe past them, and they become completely disposable.” What he wants instead is to be surrounded by photographs that inspire him, that he wishes he had taken, or whose story he half-knows – the things that remind him what he loves about the medium.

That is also the thinking behind stripping the platform of sales, followers and visible status. On the Print Swap feed, images first appear with no names attached; you only find out who took one when you tap on it. Faulkner is candid that this does not erase hierarchy so much as work around it – there is still, inevitably, a sense that some photographers carry more status than others. But that is part of what makes the swapping dynamic interesting. Do you approach someone whose work you admire but who feels out of reach, or stay within your peer group? 

Either way, he wants to guard against people simply looking out for big names. “I want it to be image-first,” he says, adding that swapping can also create a sense of recognition. “Hopefully there’s some sense of mutual appreciation. It’s always nice to have your work recognised by your peers – for them to look at it and think, that’s something I want to have around.”

“In an era where everything is commodified, particularly art, it’s refreshing to have a more democratic and affordable way to acquire prints from fellow photographers,” says Simon Roberts when asked what attracted him to the idea of Print Swap. “I’ve often swapped prints with colleagues over the years but this platform allows an opportunity to discover work by artists I might otherwise not have come across.” He adds: “The platform is very user friendly, easy to set up a profile and list work with the flexibility to create a print in the format you want, along with a nice range of archival photographic papers.”

The platform is digital, built to connect photographers wherever they are in the world, in service of something deliberately analogue – prints on a wall rather than images on a feed. “The important thing to me is the culture of swapping prints,” Faulkner says. If there were a workable way to do that without the internet, he would take it, but there usually is not – and going online opens the swaps up to people anywhere in the world. But what has surprised him most, running the platform since it launched in May, is simply how hard it is to change behaviour. People like the idea of Print Swap as soon as it is explained to them – the resistance shows up later, in actually doing it.

Faulkner compares the holdups to the friction encountered on dating apps – the reluctance to make the first move, the fear of being turned down. But, he says, “What’s the worst that can happen? Someone doesn’t want to swap with you.” Once people give it a go, they see all the things that drew him to the idea in the first place – the breadth of what other photographers are making, outside one’s immediate bubble. Faulkner compares it to the experience of walking round Photo London, stumbling on work that is not  in the books that you might  pick up in a shop, and is not what an algorithm would ever serve you.

Ultimately Faulkner hopes Print Swap encourages people to live with images, to be surrounded by work they love, at home, in the kitchen, while chopping vegetables. Done right, he thinks it is a way to democratise access, to put photographers in direct contact with the work they love.

item.title: Room share: new agency The Other Room gives female artists their own creative space - 1854 Photography
item.description:
Image © Donna Trope.

Hanna Moon, Moffy Gathorne-Hardy and Sarah Dawe join forces to set up a multigenerational agency to challenge the industry’s status quo  

The Other Room is a new agency, set up by photographer Hanna Moon, writer Moffy Gathorne-Hardy, and agent and artist advisor Sarah Dawes; its name is inspired by Virginia Woolf’s A Room of One’s Own, which argues that “A woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction”. The Other Room aims to give female creatives that space, and therefore the opportunity to pursue their work on their own terms; the opening roster includes photographers Donna Trope, Leigh Johnson, Sandy Kim, and Hanna Moon, plus artist Frances Waite.

The project includes a publishing platform, The Other Times, which features an opening essay by Gathorne-Hardy, and will soon add an interview with author Chris Kraus and an essay by curator Charlotte Cotton. Cotton helped launch the project at London’s ICA in October, in an event also featuring editor and creative consultant Isabella Burley, and writer Gem Fletcher. “It was really special,” says Moon. “It was an interesting crowd, three men out of 100 people.

“People really wanted to get advice, but also share what they thought on some quite sensitive subjects. So they asked practical questions, but also brought up topics such as shame, and why do we feel it, and how can we get through it as artists. It felt like it was a safe space, that people were able to open up.” 

“We are kind of midway, things are happening but we have to take the next step. Which is towards female ownership” – Hanna Moon

Moon and Gathorne-Hardy have worked together for about 15 years, dating back to when Gathorne-Hardy modelled and Moon liked to photograph her. Keen to set up something made for women by women they toyed with opening a gallery, then landed on an agency as “something we could do that would actually be useful”, says Gathorne-Hardy. Looking for an agent to help they “got really fucking lucky” that Dawes was interested, she adds; Dawes is a well-established industry figure, known for her long association with David Sims. “She knows how to get through the industry, and how to have a career as a mom, which is such a big part of running a female-only agency,” says Moon. “It’s inspiring to have her on our team.”

Moon is a dynamic image-maker, whose clients include brands such as British Vogue, Dazed, AnOther, Marc Jacobs, Miu Miu and Nike; she also publishes A Nice Magazine, which recently returned after a hiatus, and has included issues on the female gaze. In 2018 she joined forces with another friend, Joyce Ng, and they exhibited their work together at Somerset House. Female-only exhibitions, galleries, and editorial projects have some precedents, but a female-only agency is something new; the industry is still dominated by male photographers – and behind-the-scenes bosses and financiers – and where women photographers, and those from other underrepresented groups, have progressed they are often still underpaid. 

“Currently I think we are kind of midway, things are happening but we have to take the next step,” says Moon. “Which is towards female ownership.”

The artists represented by The Other Room span generations, including image-maker Donna Trope, who is in her seventies; this is common among female creatives, say Moon and Gathorne-Hardy, because women’s careers often do not follow linear trajectories, especially if they have had children. Part of The Other Room’s work is therefore in combating ageism, in questioning what it means to be ‘emerging’ and in reaffirming an artist’s worth after she has taken a break. Moon and Gathorne-Hardy point out that seniority can bring benefits, such as experience and knowledge, though they add it does not determine how an artist’s work looks. Trope’s images are brightly coloured and punky, says Moon; she is, says Moon, “the coolest”.

Moon and Gathorne-Hardy want to make changes, but are also realistic about the pace of change, and about everyone’s need to earn a living; they are keen to start making things happen, they say, rather than just complaining, or fantasising about dream scenarios. “We are a business, so we have to make it sustainable,” says Moon. “We have to find the balance of what can actually work in this industry. We can’t be fully punk, we still have to operate within the system, while changing it.”

“It’s not social work!” adds Gathorne-Hardy. “Everyone we have signed, we want to represent because we think they are great artists making meaningful and exciting work.” 

The Other Room is charging artists 20 per cent of their fees, a standard rate in an industry where some agencies go as high as 50 per cent; it has adopted a looser contract than the norm, allowing artists to immediately stop paying fees if they leave, rather than tying them in for months after exit. The agency has started out with five artists as this is “what we can really afford”, says Gathorne-Hardy; they are keen to keep the numbers small, so that everyone gets proper attention. They are also keen to keep the workloads manageable, rather than pushing creatives to pump work out. “That’s what I experienced when I was a fashion photographer, just working back-to-back, and then the quality goes down,” says Moon. “We want to be more strategic about what artists do.”

She believes the whole industry needs a rethink because the old business models no longer fit; she points to the time and money photographers put into making editorial shoots, arguing that they no longer necessarily win money jobs off the back of them. “We have to stop overproducing and think about where the resource is going,” she says. “Now there are key events in key cities, art fairs and fashion weeks which everyone goes to. For example, Donna is showing work in Paris Photo, so we will be there. We have to read the industry and adapt.”

item.title: The violence of immediacy: Katerina Angelopoulou advocates for justice after a deadly wildfire in a Greek town - 1854 Photography
item.description:
All images from The Fumes of Mars © Katerina Angelopoulou.

Combining first-person accounts with her own images and official documents, Katerina Angelopoulou’s The Fumes of Mars offers a counter-narrative to an unmitigated disaster.

Every era produces its own visual language and witnesses to make sense of the world. In our present moment, our visual language takes the form of hyper-accessible digital vernaculars such as screenshots and smartphone snapshots, but we still long for material anchors to prove a sense of belonging to a place, a home, a family, a community. Yet, even as we cling to these physical remnants, the terrain of perception is undergoing a radical, automated displacement, as vision detaches from the human eye and migrates into machines. Algorithms, surveillance nets and generative networks now look, interpret and act without our mediation, leaving us to wonder what will remain of witnessing when the human observer is removed from the loop entirely. 

We now live in an ecosystem that demands our constant, unblinking and mostly passive participation. This relentless flow feeds directly into what literary theorist Anna Kornbluh terms ‘immediacy’, especially when world-facts are being circulated. Kornbluh warns that our obsession with the instant, the unmediated and the direct – along with the defunding of journalism – seriously undermines our capacity for critical and collective thinking. When a systematic rejection of mediation encourages a culture of instant disavowal and superficial identification of information, the vital distance required to think and understand real-life facts collapses. 

The real violence of the contemporary image is mostly not found in its graphic content any more. True violence resides in the systematic violation of distance, the precise, contemplative buffer crucial for critical reflection. With the erasure of this space, we are deprived of the capacity to understand our world and its high-stakes politics, laws and policies. It leaves us stranded in a state of raw, unmediated chaos and mixed feelings. This erasure of distance is therefore always a deeply political act of violence.

“It became very important to make a point that you can get a more rounded and truthful story of what has happened if you don’t just take your information from one TV channel, or one government source…” –  Katerina Angelopoulou

Katerina Angelopoulou’s The Fumes of Mars engages with these factors – but also acts to reclaim distance, by gathering collective testimonies. Her work offers rigorous research into a wildfire that, on 23 July 2018, ripped through Mati, a middle-class town nestled on the eastern coast of the Attica region near Athens. The disaster claimed the lives of 104 people within hours and, years later, forensic evidence suggests another 14 to 18 unidentified people remain buried in a collective grave in the area. Angelopoulou experienced it first-hand. 

“My parents’ home was in the area – at the time, I was living in the United States, but I was visiting my mother, and that afternoon, I had just arrived,” she explains. “My mother, my daughter, who was three at the time, and I were caught by the fire directly at our doorstep. We ran with the hope and sort of the expectation that we would manage to get away and go back to Athens. But we only made it to the sea, which was just 100 metres away.”

Angelopoulou and her family stood in the sea for four to five hours as the tragedy unfolded, and the artist found herself making snapshots on her phone. “Sometimes we take pictures – or we tend to take pictures – of things that shock us, to revisit them later to make sense of what happened. I think that was what the instinct was,” she reflects. But she was only able to go through those snapshots in 2021, when she initiated an inquiry into the facts and counter-facts that led to Mati’s disaster. 

As the flames took hold, the institutional scaffolding of the state had collapsed entirely. The army, fire department, police and political leadership failed to coordinate, communicate or execute basic evacuation protocols. A secondary violence began afterwards, the violence of the state-engineered narrative. The government tried to conceal what had happened, and blame the residents for the outcome; the state, aided by uncritical media outlets, manufactured a convenient scapegoat – the residents had built illegal homes and walls, blocking access to the sea, preventing victims from escaping.

“That is the narrative that, unfortunately, was propagated by the media, which had no specific information about the area, but just used it as a shield,” Angelopoulou notes. “And over time, it became part of the collective unconscious.” She monitored international media reports, read every scrap of public testimony, and examined the official statements of government bodies. The day after the fire, the Minister of Internal Affairs had publicly claimed there were no operational mistakes. It was an outright lie; data later revealed that officials knew the scope of the tragedy while downplaying it in real-time.

Angelopoulou’s approach pieces together a counter-narrative from survivor testimonies, collected via public sources such as newspapers, television interviews and social media posts, alongside more personal photographs from the catastrophe and the aftermath. The Fumes of Mars juxtaposes images of the charred interiors of Mati’s homes alongside expansive, eerie landscapes, and written testimonies from the survivors. 

“I wanted to make sure that everything that is in there can be found elsewhere,” she says. “It became very important to make a point that you can get a more rounded and truthful story of what has happened if you don’t just take your information from one TV channel, or one government source, or one newspaper, and go through a number of news channels or information channels. Politicians and politics have always had an agenda.” 

Weaving her personal images with maps tracking the fire’s geographical spread, and matching these pairings against the recorded movements of police and fire engines, Angelopoulou built an iron-clad, forensic timeline exposing the flaws of the official timeline, and the system faults that had occurred. The Fumes of Mars transcends digital forensics to trace a profound parable of the “last image” – the very last image one records, as could have been the case for Angelopoulou, shooting from the chaos of the fire. It maps the evolution of a visual remnant, from the raw, instinctual impulse to document an unfolding catastrophe, and from within elements of immediacy culture, to its role in the quiet aftermath of survival, and finally, to its creative reconstruction.

By examining what a last image can still signify and accomplish, the work also illuminates the long journey of making sense of trauma, which for Angelopoulou led to a deeply personal excavation of her late father’s belongings. “I went back and collected things from the house and photographed them as archaeological remnants, where one can just recount one’s life,” she explains. Isolating charred objects and documenting them with deliberate, forensic composure, Angelopoulou transforms them into monuments of survival and loss. 

For her, the physical destruction of her family home symbolised a deeper erasure of identity. “Losing the house I grew up in, the house I always went back to was devastating,” she says. “It’s probably the place where I have the most memories of my parents, because they were so busy during the year that summers were the only time we actually saw them. It’s also the place where I hold the most memories of my father. I think that’s partly why the loss of that house, that area, and that place felt, in the biggest sense, like a loss of where I came from.”

Reclaiming this lost horizon through her practice, Angelopoulou suggests that the truthfulness of photography lives on in this capacity for restoring context, history and analytical depth to human suffering – even from images produced by the immediacy culture that Kornbluh frames. The Fumes of Mars posits this last image as a foundation upon which to reclaim collective memory and political critique; crucial to this reclamation is dismantling of the institutional monopoly on truth, through a deliberate engagement with the ‘unreliable witness’. 

In legal and psychological discourse, a single witness to a trauma is routinely dismissed as unreliable, vulnerable to shock and fragmented perception. The state weaponises this scepticism, omitting community stories under the guise of maintaining objective order, while propagating its own fabricated narrative. Angelopoulou flips this dynamic on its head by gathering a constellation of disparate survivor testimonies; individuals who had no way of coordinating their accounts, describe the exact same breakdown of state apparatus from completely different geographical vantage points. The singular, unreliable witness dissolves into a reliable, collective truth.

This plurivocal approach shifts authority away from the singular, top-down governmental decree and returns it to the community, lending a complex, dual utility to the raw, unedited smartphone snaps circulating in the immediate aftermath of the fire. The least manipulated, most democratic archives of the unfolding event, these images possess a slippery elasticity; a photograph can amplify a scene to look more apocalyptic than it was, or conversely, flatten an end-of-the-world reality into something seemingly manageable. A single image is never enough. But when these raw visual fragments are tethered to a rigorous, cross-referenced network of collective testimonies they shed their ambiguity.

item.title: Valérie Belin and the objects that outlive us - 1854 Photography
item.description:
Portrait of Valérie Belin. ©Louise Lenepveu

As her Prix Pictet-winning Still Life series returns to view at Paris Photo, the French artist considers consumer excess, the persistence of plastic and the allure of beauty.

The objects in Valérie Belin’s photographs have little purpose beyond being looked at. Decorative ornaments, artificial pearls, a mask or a mirror become the components of elaborate arrangements whose glossy surfaces and insistent colour suggest a world of extravagant abundance. The photographs borrow the authority of still-life painting, giving cheap consumer goods the appearance of treasures. Their troubling quality emerges when we consider how little these things matter to us, and how long they might remain.

“They are made of plastic, a material that has something paradoxical about it,” Belin tells BJP. “It is artificial, yet almost indestructible. It gives these insignificant objects a kind of grotesque immortality.”

Made in 2014, Still Life won the sixth Prix Pictet the following year, for the cycle themed ‘Disorder’. This month, it will be presented alongside Alfredo Jaar’s The End at Paris Photo, as Pictet Group begins its official partnership with the fair. The two series bring different forms of environmental concern into dialogue: Jaar’s photographs of Utah’s diminishing Great Salt Lake and Belin’s studio constructions of manufactured excess.

Belin’s pictures draw on the vanitas, a tradition of still-life painting in which possessions, perishable foods and reminders of death invite reflection on the brevity of life. Her contemporary version disturbs that relationship between the human lifespan and the things that fill it.

“In traditional vanitas, objects remind us of the transience of life. Here, they seem destined to survive us,” she says. “This is an immortality that is slowly destroying the world in which we live.”

The series examines consumer culture through the visual appeal of its objects. Colour, gloss and the relationships between objects draw us into compositions whose richness seems out of proportion to their contents. Belin wanted to create images that were seductive, artificial and disturbing, allowing their implications to appear through the experience of looking.

“In my work, the human figure can become an object, just as an object can acquire a kind of presence”

Valérie Belin

 

“The meaning emerges from the tension between the beauty of the composition and what it represents,” she explains.

That tension connects Still Life with a wider practice in which appearances repeatedly unsettle our understanding of the subject. The Paris-based artist’s photographs of people and mannequins have long questioned the distinction between a living presence and its manufactured likeness. Across portraits and objects, the surface becomes a place where we struggle to establish what, or who, we are encountering.

“In my work, the human figure can become an object, just as an object can acquire a kind of presence,” she says.

In Mannequins (2003), the first impression of a living model gives way to the recognition of a shop-window dummy. Details of texture and construction undo the illusion. This movement between recognition and doubt is central to her work: the camera records a surface with great precision, while making our understanding of what lies behind it less secure.

Within Still Life, mannequin heads, arms and hands become elements in the arrangements, placed almost on the same terms as everything surrounding them. Their fragmented bodies imply an unsettling consequence of accumulation: the person disappears into the possessions.

“I wanted to suggest a human presence that has been absorbed, suffocated or buried beneath this accumulation,” Belin explains. “The distinction between the human and the artificial becomes uncertain.”

Yet the apparent chaos is meticulously organised. Belin selects and arranges her objects according to relationships of form, colour, material and light. She describes the contradiction as an ordered image evoking a world that has lost its balance, with the compositions suggesting an unfamiliar galaxy or a new form of life. Disorder becomes something capable of generating its own logic.

Winning the Prix Pictet expanded the audience for these questions, placing the series within a wider discussion about sustainability. Founded in 2008, the prize recognises photography engaging with environmental and social concerns. Belin values the way this context allows different aspects of her work to be considered together: its formal construction, its relationship with art history and its representation of consumer society.

“These different readings are not contradictory; they are all part of the work,” she says.

More than a decade later, she sees continuity in the pictures, even as their context has shifted. Plastic’s persistence and the consequences of mass consumption have become harder to ignore. “What changes is the context in which we look at them.”

The uncertainty running through her photographs also acquires a different resonance amid the rise of generative AI. Belin has always understood photography as transformative: lighting, framing and composition make something new from what the camera records. The encounter with an actual subject nevertheless remains essential to her process.

“I am interested in its materiality, its surface and the way light acts upon it,” she says. “The ambiguity of the image begins with something real.”

Belin makes no claim that a photograph must explain a problem or supply its solution. Its usefulness may lie in creating an encounter whose implications take time to become clear. Drawn towards these arrangements before fully understanding them, we have the opportunity to examine our own attraction.

“Perhaps the images invite us to look again at the objects that surround us, and to question the place they occupy in our lives.”

Valérie Belin’s Still Life and Alfredo Jaar’s The End will be presented by Prix Pictet on the Promenoir at Paris Photo, Grand Palais, 12–15 November 2026, with a preview on 11 November.

item.title: Masha Sviatahor on how archival images disrupt political narratives in her series Promised Butterflies - 1854 Photography
item.description:
All images from the series Promised Butterflies © Masha Sviatahor.

Masha Sviatahor is a Belarusian artist working with photography, archival materials, collage and photomontage. Her practice explores history, collective memory, and questions of power and ideology. Her first book, Everybody Dance! (2025), was published by TAMAKA. Her work has been exhibited at Yale University and Circulation(s) Festival, and she was named a BJP One to Watch in 2021. Here, she discusses her practice in her own words.

“I’ve been working with Soviet photographic archives since 2018. In my earlier works I was interested in repetition, fragmentation, dismantling and reassembling familiar motifs – ballerinas, workers, soldiers, political leaders – as a way of investigating how their original ideological meanings could be undermined and recontextualised. With Promised Butterflies, my focus shifted more directly towards images of political power and collective unity.

What first drew me to these archives was their visual language. I became fascinated by how carefully these photographs were constructed: the choreography of bodies, gestures and expressions, the recurring compositions, the precision with which every element seems to reinforce the others. Although I work with Soviet archival material, my interest extends beyond that particular historical moment. The archive is really a point of entry into broader questions about how images shape collective perception, construct ideas of order and authority, and produce shared belief.

The photographs I use depict carefully orchestrated collective rituals, an idealised façade of power and society. What struck me wasn’t only how widely these images circulated, but how strongly they resembled one another. That repetition is essential because it creates familiarity. Particular visual ideas are repeated until they begin to feel natural or inevitable. Spectacle makes those ideas emotionally persuasive. Political power often operates through these visual strategies, not simply by telling people what to think, but by shaping how reality itself is seen and experienced.

I approach these archival photographs as constructions, as systems built through repetition, omission and visual discipline. What interests me is creating a situation where these endlessly reproduced political ceremonies and images of collective unity begin to lose their stability. In Promised Butterflies I introduce an element that interrupts the internal logic of the image and reveals how vulnerable these systems actually are. Something that initially appears coherent, unified and controlled starts to fracture. The image no longer functions as a stable whole.

“I want the tension between the original photograph and my intervention to remain visible because the work emerges through that encounter. I’m not adding truth”  – Masha Sviatahor

It’s also difficult to know whether transformation becomes stuck, whether it’s endlessly deferred, or whether it takes place in a distorted way, producing these alien, disproportionate and unsettling forms through which monumental political scenes suddenly begin to appear fragile. A giant caterpillar appearing on a party tribune makes the entire political ritual feel temporary, staged and theatrical. It almost becomes an image of political spectacle itself.

What interests me is the collision between two different modes operating within the work. On one side there is politics, with its aspiration towards control, stability and permanence. On the other there is the organic, which follows its own logic and can never be completely controlled. Images of power often contain something that resists their own internal order. The forms I introduce simply make that resistance visible.

The title Promised Butterflies points to the gap between what is promised and what is ultimately delivered. In the Soviet context there was a constant promise of change, progress and a brighter future. Those promises were sustained through ideology, images and collective rituals, yet there was always a discrepancy between how that future was represented and how it was actually experienced. Change certainly happened, but it never coincided with the utopian future that had been promised. Transformation failed to fulfil its own promise. Instead it appeared as simulation, distortion or failure. Promises became visual constructions that remained unrealised.

That tension feels equally present today. Political systems continue to produce narratives of renewal and progress, but the question is how those narratives materialise in practice and what kinds of realities they actually produce. We live in a period of continuous transformation that is often impossible to fully comprehend or control. At the same time, we seem to exist in a prolonged state of expectation; waiting for wars to end, for authoritarian regimes to collapse, for violence to cease. Those transformations are repeatedly postponed, interrupted or emerge in distorted forms. Transformation never fully conforms to the systems that seek to organise or appropriate it.

Working with photographs made by other people inevitably raises questions of authorship, but for me it begins with the archive itself. The images I work with are not neutral. They were created as instruments of ideology. They didn’t simply document the world, they helped shape what people were encouraged to believe and how history itself was understood.

My role isn’t to claim authority over those images or erase them. I want the tension between the original photograph and my intervention to remain visible because the work emerges through that encounter. I’m not adding truth. Instead I create a layer through which what has been excluded or suppressed can return – not literally, but as something that was never supposed to appear. Rather than analysing these systems from a distance, I intervene in them physically, revealing not propaganda itself, but the mechanisms through which it operates and eventually begins to break down.

These photographs also changed the way I think about the period they come from. I worked mainly with the archives of Sovetskoe Foto [at one time the only photography magazine in the Soviet Union, founded in 1926 and published in Moscow], material that had already been selected, edited and arranged within broader ideological frameworks. Gradually I became more aware of recurring visual structures through which particular values were communicated. I became increasingly interested in the tensions, inconsistencies and omissions concealed within these apparently stable systems. The archive stopped feeling like a fixed record of history and became something that could be reopened, questioned and read differently.”

item.description:
All images from the series A Circle of 12 Gold Stars on a Blue Background © Jan Staiger.

Taking the familiar blue and gold tropes that represent the European Union, the German-born photographer explores the visuality of the complex constructs of the Commission with his project A Circle of 12 Gold Stars on a Blue Background

Depictions of the European Union are often limited to a handful of recurring themes – close-ups of European Commission leaders on podiums, renderings of glass-heavy institutional building facades, obsessive picturings of the Union’s waving blue flag. Jan Staiger is attempting to photograph the bureaucratic machinery of the EU with the same image conventions, his project A Circle of 12 Gold Stars on a Blue Background restaging the Union’s determined types, while flipping its visual language.

Created across four European countries – Belgium, Germany, France and Greece – A Circle of 12 Gold Stars on a Blue Background traces the tropes of EU political communication. Idealised self-images and self-picturings, these representations are often far from the realities of the place. “I see the European district in Brussels as a sort of imaginary political green screen,” says Staiger, who was born in the German city Nuremberg, but is now based in Brussels, where the EU has its headquarters. “If you walk 20 minutes further, you see all the issues European capitals face displayed on the street.”

“I see the European district in Brussels as a sort of imaginary political green screen” – Jan Staiger

Staiger’s photographic record is constrained, partly through necessity. While working in European Commission buildings, photographers are watched by press officers, he says, adding, “you’re never alone”. They are also forced to follow the Commission’s protocols as laid out in its Visual Identity Manual. Staiger turns these protocols against themselves, his images made ghostly by sharp artificial light, the staged EU regalia emptied of its performative energy.

In one striking shot, 10 blue balloons – each printed with the ring of 12 gold stars – bob in the rough waters off Lesbos, Greece. The island has been central to EU migration policy since 2015, when it became an arrival point for hundreds of thousands crossing from Turkey. Staiger’s balloons read as iconographic buoys, EU symbolism set adrift within the migration crisis its politics have yet to resolve.

Staiger began A Circle of 12 Gold Stars on a Blue Background during his MA studies at KASK School of Arts in Ghent, and the series perhaps takes its most concentrated form in his book of the same name. Designed around the European Commission Visual Identity Manual, it is bound like an official document stack, and carries the title in all 24 official EU languages. The publication’s laser-cut cover references an overlooked alternative design for the European flag, stars scattered in the member states’ rough geographical positions, not the neat, equalising circle there is today.

This alternative flag hints at Staiger’s hopes for the EU and its visual representation, which is for reform not complete overhaul. “I’m not naive,” he says. “I cannot change an entire media landscape.”

item.title: Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize 2027 shortlist pushes the boundaries of the medium - 1854 Photography
item.description:
Untitled, 2023. From the series Death by GPS, 2022–2026 © Salvatore Vitale.

Hoda Afshar, Lotus L Kang, Sasha Kurmaz and Salvatore Vitale are shortlisted for the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize 2027

Hoda Afshar, Lotus L Kang, Sasha Kurmaz and Salvatore Vitale have been shortlisted for the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize 2027. Recognising artists from anywhere in the world for exhibitions or books in Europe which have made a significant contribution to photography in the preceding year, the award is celebrated for spotlighting outstanding and innovative work. The exhibition of selected work from the four artists’ shortlisted projects will be at The Photographers’ Gallery, London, from 10 March to 06 June 2027, before moving to the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation in Eschborn/Frankfurt from 19 June to 26 September 2027. The winner of the £30,000 prize will be announced in April 2027.

Hoda Afshar, who was born in 1983 in Tehran, Iran, is shortlisted for the exhibition Performing the Invisible at the Musée du Quai Branly – Jacques Chirac, Paris, France, which used images, drawings, videos, mirrors and sound to interrogate photography’s role in colonialism, and as a tool for resistance. At the centre of the exhibition was The Fold, which worked with the archive of French psychiatrist and photographer Gaëtan Gatian de Clérambault (1872–1934), and the thousands of photographs of veiled individuals – mostly women – he made in Morocco. 

“Such archives are never about the subject,” Afshar told BJP in our December 2025 issue. “They’re about the purpose the colonial photography was serving – to classify, to justify colonisation.” Afshar’s exhibition in Paris added further elements such as video interviews.

“The 2027 Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize shortlist represents the expansiveness of photography and how it’s used to explore ideas of resistance, conflict, memory and identity in our contemporary age”
– Shoair Mavlian

Sasha Kurmaz, born in 1986 in Kyiv, Ukraine, is shortlisted for the publication Red Horse, published by Éditions Images Vevey in November 2025. Kurmaz began the project following the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and his 800-page publication brings together handmade collages, documentary photographs, notes, drawings and newspaper cuttings to create a diaristic insight into the experience of war, and his reflection on how photography can – or cannot – communicate this experience to others. 

“Red Horse is not just a photography book, it is a deeply personal story of my life, documented and embodied through artistic means,” Kurmaz has stated. “War is a machine for turning personalities into abstraction,” he writes in Red Horse, which was designed by Nicholas Polli and won the  2026 Kraszna-Krausz Photography Book Award.

Salvatore Vitale, born in 1986 in Palermo, Italy, is shortlisted for the exhibition SABOTAGE at Photo Elysée, Lausanne, Switzerland (06 March–31 May 2026), which questions systems of automation and surveillance by collaborating with the precariously employed people working to sustain this economy. Working with South African freelancers, Vitale considers how digital infrastructures reproduce historical and colonial patterns of extraction, exploitation and inequality, and how photography can reveal and critique this system – but also be part of the problem. 

“This kind of analysis is very much in relation to understanding what kind of act of sabotage – even if very subtle – can exist,” Vitale told BJP in March 2026. “It doesn’t have to be activism, but how can we build different narratives or look at those topics from different perspectives?”

Lotus L Kang, born in 1985 in Toronto, Canada, is shortlisted for the exhibition The face of desire is loss, which was shown in the Bulgari Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, Italy (09 May–22 November 2026). Combining photography, film and sculpture, this show immersed the viewer in lengths of unfixed photographic film – which Kang calls ‘skins’ – suspended from steel joists; it also included 49 bottles of spirits, which represent the days a soul spends between death and rebirth in Buddhist belief, as well as sculptures of tatami mats and cast objects in plaster, bronze and fibreglass depicting crying birds and kelp knots, evoking the body in states of rest, dream, recovery and death. Together they symbolise the flux of life and impermanence. 

The jury for the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize 2027 was: Laia Abril, multidisciplinary artist; Damarice Amao, associate curator for photography at the Musée National d’Art Moderne / Centre Pompidou; Verónica Fieiras, artist, editor and publisher (CHACO); Anne-Marie Beckmann, director of Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation, and Shoair Mavlian, director of The Photographers’ Gallery, as voting chair.

“As we reach the 30th anniversary of the prize giving, the 2027 Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize shortlist represents the expansiveness of photography and how it’s used to explore ideas of resistance, conflict, memory and identity in our contemporary age,” commented Mavlian on the shortlist.

item.title: Star turn: Misan Harriman on photography, celebrity and activism - 1854 Photography
item.description:
Still Waiting for Justice, London, 14 June 2024 © Misan Harriman.

Eminent photographer, global activist and cultural thinker, Misan Harriman refuses “to become politically mute in exchange for acceptance”. He speaks to Isaac Huxtable

Misan Harriman has a captive audience. Five years ago the London-based portrait photographer was an extremely established practitioner, top of his game, magazine covers across the newsstands, the man selected for Meghan and Harry Sussex’s baby announcement (and baby reveal). A proud and politically active Black man, Harriman was a shining exemplar in shifting editorial times. Black Lives Matter had shaken the fashion/editorial/publication worlds, and essential, overdue attention was being given to Black artists, celebrities, thinkers, politicians. Often they were photographed by Harriman. He has worked with Steve McQueen, Lewis Hamilton, Diane Abbott, Naomi Campbell and Marcus Rashford, to name but a few. He is also the first Black photographer in the century-long history of British Vogue to shoot the September issue cover. In July 2021, he became chair of the Southbank Centre, London. 

Harriman built a platform and audience throughout his rise, attracting people who appreciate the twin flames of artistic production and political activism. He is a star photographer. But his Blackness, his politics, his belief in human value, and the actual point of all this representation is rooted in Black political thought. Sometimes the sumptuous photograph and the vocal photographer do not mix with ease, as was the case for Gordon Parks, one of his inspirations. Harriman is a man of principles, and principles have a cost. He knows why he makes these photographs, and he refuses to be silenced. A week after this interview, amid calls for Harriman to be removed from his position as chair of the Southbank Centre due to social media posts, the photographer announced he will not seek another term. He will step down this autumn.

“It’s my job to represent the human condition. And also, for me as a human being, I do not believe that there can ever be a child of a lesser God” – Misan Harriman

Isaac Huxtable: At this year’s Photo London, you presented The Purpose of Light, an all-encompassing display of portraits taken at protests, heavily featuring activism against the genocide in Gaza and the British government’s role in the ongoing conflict, but also Black Lives Matter, trans rights protests and environmental activism. Photo London is a fair, where people walk around mingling, looking at pictures for sale. Your booth stopped many in their tracks, and created this major interruption to the pleasant, glittery cycles of such fairs. It was hotly discussed and impossible to avoid. Can you tell me more about that? 

Misan Harriman: I wish I could take the credit for this one, but it’s all in the brilliance of my gallerist, Aki Abiola, and his Hope 93 gallery. I had offers to include some of the prints in maybe a group show, but we realised what we could do with a proper space at Photo London. Aki said, we don’t always get this captive audience, so let’s remind them what’s going on in a world that is, frankly, on fire, right? We have a chance to make them remember the trans community, climate action, women’s rights, the queer community, Black Lives, Gaza, Iran, Afghanistan, you know, all of it – Grenfell, for God’s sake, Grenfell – and see the intersectionality of the work, shot over seven years in three continents. 

It also points to the legacy of Civil Rights photography, the importance of looking at the documentation of protest, or a world on fire. When people think about Cecil Beaton, for example, they might think about the glamour, the royals. But he also shot the Blitz. It’s about how we choose where we point our lens. But when the world is in the place it is now, I think we have to bear witness in the way that I’m trying to force people to do. For work like this, it’s really, really important for it to live in the art world in a way that, as you’ve said, it often doesn’t. 

IH: What was the reception?

MH: It was an extremely busy booth the entire fair. The work wasn’t overwhelming, but it was immersive. It’s an overtly political body of work at a very divisive time. And we didn’t know whether there would be, you know, complaints, letters, calls to the people that run [Photo London] to shut it down. But we did know the art has to do the work. As an artist you need to let the work be in the places that it can have the most impact. And then, it was extraordinary. There was a lot of emotion and loads of feedback saying that it was their favourite booth, a reminder of so much that’s going on. 

I’ll be honest with you, for a lot of Black and Brown people, to see themselves represented in this way, in this place… The fine art world doesn’t always make people of colour feel necessarily welcomed. And to have a Black gallerist with a Black artist, with many Black and Brown and Muslim people on the walls, was cathartic and deeply healing for a lot of people. A lot of people were crying. I don’t know if people cry in art fairs.

IH: You mention Cecil Beaton, and I know Gordon Parks is a very important photographer for you. I’m struck that they’re both photographers who were able to balance glamour and beauty with perhaps more political, polemic happenings, from the Blitz to the Civil Rights Movement. Parks sits between genres – he’s now seen in a gallery context, but he was working for magazines, while doing something very documentary, something for the advancement of Black Americans.

MH: Yes, Parks is my idol. It’s exactly that ability to carry your political voice into your practice, and not compromise. The active choice to turn your lens on to the ills of this wounded planet. It would have been easy for me just to do big shows of my celebrity portrait portfolio – Harrison Ford, Kate Winslet, Jay-Z. But look outside, people! All of our rights are under attack. To look at my archive and decide to just show my celebrity work? That’s just not an option. That’s not how I’ve been raised, it’s not how I feel. I’m a child of the Empire. I understand what it means historically for art to have a voice. Nina Simone’s quote always comes back to me saying, ‘An artist’s duty is to reflect the times that we’re living in. Everything else is entertainment’. We have enough entertainment.

IH: With these intentions, your platforms, your images and your voice, you also have to balance being an institutional stakeholder, a public figure. You also have to work. How do you manage all that on a global stage?

MH: I think of Omar El Akkad’s book, which changed my life in many ways, One Day, Everyone Will Have Always Been Against This. It really helped centre myself as the world became even more divisive, and I needed to remember what my practice must be. It’s my job to represent the human condition. And also, for me as a human being, I do not believe that there can ever be a child of a lesser God. I know that if I walked out of my front door and there was a child bleeding on the floor, I’m not going to ask that child who their God is. I’m not going to check what colour skin they have. I’m going to help that child. So I think it’s a combination of many things. 

I can’t call up the world leaders, but my photographs can cross borders instantly. Someone said to me, forget photography, they can’t think of any artists alive today that reach as many people as I do online. So it’s well past me just being a photographer that people talk about. My voice has become part of the practice. When people see a 48-year-old Black man crying, weeping over whatever horror I’ve seen that day, I think is why there’s real trust in my voice. I’m not this generation of influencer that’s trying to tell everyone that I can walk on water, that I have all the answers. But if I hear of a child that’s been shot by a sniper, that’s going to break me. 

I am a father myself, above and beyond an artist. How can we allow that to be normalised, how has apathy taken dominion over us to a point where you can see that on your phone and then you worry about whether you’re getting Glastonbury tickets this summer? I have a voice, and I have a camera. 

The Voice newspaper did an article and they said, as chair of the board of Southbank, I represent something increasingly rare in British cultural life – a prominent Black cultural figure occupying institutional space while refusing to become politically mute in exchange for acceptance. As an artist, my voice is my voice. I can make it very clear the platform I am speaking on behalf of. It’s really clear to anyone that follows me that when you see me crying over dead children in Congo or Gaza, that’s me, Misan Harriman, responding to the ills of the world. And I think that’s something that most people would accept as very normal. 

IH: Thinking about how this political belief is embedded into your whole practice, I’m curious to hear your approach to the specificity of a Black photographer shooting Black subjects.

MH: It’s interesting you ask this because I did a post a few weeks ago of Black men and women portraits I’ve taken. It was in response to people saying there’s something about the way I shoot Black people. In Nigeria we have a saying, that we see ourselves. I don’t know if there is a training manual for trust, and ultimately I think it’s that. I’ve shot Steve McQueen many times and we have an unspoken language. He arrives on set, we kick it, we talk, we know what it is. And it’ll be a look, and he’s like, have you got it? And I’ll say, yeah I got it… 

I don’t know how else to be. It’s not technical. I think the conversation before can sometimes make the image. An understanding of the shared lived experience can make the subject give more than they would with another person who doesn’t really understand what life is like for them. And then lighting. I use natural light. I understand how, the massive spectrum of natural light and how it falls on Black skin. And that’s just built in. I just know how to do that. So it’s a combination of understanding light and how melanin reacts to light within the subjects, and then the unspoken, almost spiritual trust.

item.title: Matthew Connors confronts a challenging modern world in The Axe Will Survive the Master - 1854 Photography
item.description:
Image from The Axe Will Survive the Master © Matthew Connors.

The third in a trilogy of photobooks, collating images made over 12 years, Matthew Connors’ latest work asks demanding questions of a world facing violence and uncertainty

“The axe is always there, ready. The master’s axe… survives everything. Don’t ever forget it.” These words were spoken by a former executioner for the NKVD (the Soviet secret police) and recorded by Svetlana Alexievich in Secondhand Time: The Last of the Soviets, her epic oral history on the collapse of the USSR. Matthew Connors evokes the sentiment for something even more ambitious; a photographic insight into our contemporary world, made over 12 years in cities such as Bangkok, Cairo, Chernobyl, Hong Kong, Kyiv, Naples, Pyongyang, Varanasi and Washington DC.

There is a danger that such a sprawling topic can dissipate into nothing – if something is about everything is it about anything? – but Connors keeps the narrative tight. The opening pages focus on flat planes and ads and images in public space, the narrative then expands out to scenes of violence and repression. The book is divided into chapters such as ‘Maculate Origins’ (maculate is the opposite of immaculate) or ‘A Caucus of Shadows’. It is often hard to judge where Connors has taken particular shots, suggesting that the many locations have much in common; globalisation has flattened differences between cultures, the same clothes, technology and rising authoritarianism mapping onto everywhere.

It is often hard to judge where Connors has taken particular shots, suggesting that the many locations have much in common

The book cover is intriguing, depicting glass smashed into a circle that also suggests a camera lens; there is maybe a metacriticism at work here, in which the camera is part of the problem. The photographs show a reality fracturing partly because of images, billboards and reflections intersecting with flat planes and fragments of views; meanwhile laser pointers and masks document attempts to evade surveillance. Connors’ text, The Knotted Alliance, is written in first-person plural (‘we’) and describes a petition annotated and updated by many hands; it refers to a group effort. There is something interesting going on around the group versus the individual, the ability to reach a consensus, or – as in Alexievich’s case – to gather many voices. 

Where Connors’ images fit into that is moot. Does his assemblage of scenes suggest a sense of the polyvocal? Or the organising perspective of his particular vision of things? Does the camera allow us to think of the individual point of view or – as Donna Haraway had it – encourage a “god trick” in which everything is apparently seen from nowhere? Conclusions are not easy to draw, but this book is asking the big questions, and making a case for their urgency.

item.title: The home front: Rémy Artiges on photographing French far-right politician Jean-Marie Le Pen - 1854 Photography
item.description:
Jean-Marie Le Pen at his home, 26 June 2019 © Rémy Artiges.

With the polls predicting an election win for the Rassemblement Nationale next April, France’s far right is closing in on power. Rémy Artiges discusses photographing the party’s founder Jean-Marie Le Pen, from his first inklings of success to his later years.

France’s next presidential election is scheduled for April 2027 and so far the polls indicate Rassemblement Nationale will win; if so it will be the first time the far right has been in power in France since 1945, and the impact will ripple across Europe and beyond. “It’s a mess!” says Rémy Artiges. “French politics is super divided at the moment, and I am sure that the traditional right wing would prefer to join the far right than the far left [in the event of a coalition]. So the RN could win next year.” 

It has been a long road for the RN, which was known until 2018 as Le Front National. It started in 1972, when the neo-fascist Ordre Nouveau joined with Jean-Marie Le Pen’s growing political movement; already a veteran of far-right politics, who had called for collaborationists to be rehabilitated, Le Pen headed the party from the start. Standing in the French presidential election of 1974, he won just 0.74 per cent of the vote, but in the intervening time the political centre has shifted. And while similar shifts have occurred the world over, in France this move is particularly associated with Le Pen. In fact the process of mainstreaming far-right-wing thinking was dubbed ‘la lepénisation’ in the 1980s.

Le Pen’s daughter Marine took over in 2011 and claimed to ‘de-demonise’ the party, expelling her father in 2015 after he (again) described the Nazi gas chambers as a “detail” of World War Two. Marine renamed the party and RN is now described as ‘populist right’ by some outlets, though it is still accused of promoting xenophobia, especially Islamophobia. In 2018 Steve Bannon, former adviser to Donald Trump, gave a speech to RN members, stating: “Let them call you racist, let them call you xenophobes, let them call you nativists. Wear it like a badge of honour. Because every day, we get stronger and they get weaker… History is on our side and will bring us victory.” The members gave him a standing ovation. 

“The far-right movement and neo-fascists have won in many ways all around the world,” observes Artiges. “Even if they’re not directly in power, their politics is the centre of attention.”

“The far right movement and neo-fascists have won in many ways all around the world. Even if they’re not directly in power, their politics is the centre of attention” – Rémy Artiges

Artiges first met Jean-Marie Le Pen in 2002, after being sent to photograph him by left-leaning newspaper Libération during another presidential election campaign. Initially Artiges refused the assignment, “because the closer you get, the more impacted you are”, and because of an ongoing debate about publicising Le Pen and his ideas. “At that time Jean-Marie Le Pen was considered unacceptable by most of the political and media community,” Artiges explains. “What he was saying was way beyond the limit of the law, he was taken to court so many times for antisemitism, racism, and negationism [for example, Holocaust denial]. So people did not want to give him space. There was an ethical issue, ‘Do you want to give space to his horrible thoughts?’”

Le Pen had complained about this exclusion in the early 1980s, writing to President Mitterrand to protest the “media boycott” against his party; the president instructed the main television channels to give the FN equitable coverage, and in February 1984 Le Pen appeared on prime-time TV for the first time. He later described this as “the hour that changed everything”, and his charisma and sheer force of personality immediately attracted attention among voters. “He was before social media, from another century, but he had that same ability to occupy space,” says Artiges. “Whatever he said, he said loud and proud because he really believed in it all. But he also wanted to shock you. That was his way to operate. He was like a black hole sucking in the light.”

Artiges agreed to cover Le Pen’s campaign but stick to straight documentary, shooting exactly what he saw, not portraits or caricature. When he arrived he found he and his fellow photojournalists were uninspired, most of them just doing the job. Then, on the very first day, there came a shock. Le Pen had won an unexpected 16.86 per cent of the first round vote – second place after the incumbent President Jacques Chirac, and enough to go through to the second round. It was the first time someone so far to the right had got that far in France, and a major political event. Artiges’ images capture some of the visceral reaction in the FN camp.

“They were hysterical!” he says. “Super, super happy because finally their ideas were being recognised. Previously Le Pen had been kind of a political outcast, now they could see some power. So they were overjoyed, but also there was a sense of violence. In general they weren’t polite, especially to me because I was from Libération and that wasn’t their favourite paper. But I believe physical violence, men who play on their physical abilities, is part of the far right. It’s part of the deal.” 

Artiges stayed with the FN campaign, still trying to simply document; his images capture the media circus around Le Pen, the microphones amplifying his thoughts and policies, the political posters declaring him president. A low point was photographing an event at which a group of kids watched admiringly as Le Pen spoke, he says. Wider public opinion was united against Le Pen, however, and parties across the political spectrum joined together to campaign against him for the second vote. Slogans circulated such as ‘A crook is better than a fascist’ (‘Un escroc mieux qu’un facho’) and ‘Graft rather than hate, Chirac rather than Le Pen’ (‘L’arnaque plutôt que la haine, Chirac plutôt que Le Pen’) and – while anti-Le Pen rather than pro-Chirac – they helped the standing president win 82 per cent of the vote, the biggest majority since the Fifth Republic was established in 1958. 

Artiges photographed the FN until the end of the election then told Libération he would stop; more widely, Le Pen once again exited the limelight. The following years saw the politician revert to bête noire, especially after his daughter became leader and expelled him from the party. In 2017 Marine reached the second round in the presidential election, winning 33 per cent of the vote, then in 2019 Jean-Marie Le Pen announced he would retire, and Libération asked Artiges to shoot him again. This time the deal was different, the newspaper requesting a formal portrait to accompany a written interview, and Artiges keenly aware he was photographing a 90-year-old. “I had the same reservations as before, and he hadn’t changed,” he says. “But I felt I had to pay attention to the fact that he was an old man. I wasn’t going to shoot the ambulance [kick someone when they were down].”

Le Pen welcomed the publicity; he still had that sense of ego, Artiges says, the desire to be centre of attention. Artiges and the writer Tristan Berteloot went to Le Pen’s home in a wealthy suburb and – while not the home built by Napoleon III, given to Le Pen by a French industrialist in 1977 – it was lavish. In fact it was “over-decorated and over-lit”, says Artiges, and it was a hot day so all the shutters were closed. Faced with electric lighting and an elderly subject who needed to sit for the shoot, his first concerns were “empirical” questions around how to make a portrait at all. Finding a bucolic mural, he instinctively used it as a backdrop; posing in front with a black shirt and grim expression, Le Pen somehow embodies curmudgeonly ire.

“It’s the contrast between the pastoral, green background and Le Pen,” says Artiges. “I put him in a comfortable situation but he can’t help himself. I took another portrait in front of a painting but it’s less disturbing, I think because the blue background is more relatable. But it’s still interesting because it features dogs that look like something northern European, even Aryan, and that was in his home.” 

Two years later Artiges was invited to photograph Le Pen again, as Marine and the party he had founded reached the second round of the presidential election once more. Le Pen was now in declining health, having had a heart attack earlier in 2022, but his iron will – and infamous charisma – were undiminished. The images look like reportage but were actually carefully stage-managed by Le Pen and his team, says Artiges; his apparently candid shots of Le Pen holding forth over a drink were closely duplicated by other photographers surveying the scene because, positioned in front of the politician like an audience, they were encouraged to watch him perform. Another image shows Le Pen and his wife watching TV as the second round vote was announced; the screen shows Macron winning, as had been predicted. Artiges suspects Le Pen wanted the press to record his daughter’s defeat. 

At the same time, this photograph also records a near miss. Marine had won 42 per cent in the second round, a once unthinkable result for the party Le Pen founded and maybe a promise of more to come. “If we gain 10 points every [presidential election], next time, we’ll win,” noted Marine’s protege, Jordan Bardella, on French TV. Le Pen was backing Eric Zemmour not Marine, but perhaps was gratified nonetheless.

These images were some of the last taken of Le Pen, who died in 2025. The man has passed away, but his politics, ideas and images live on. “The media has a responsibility in constructing power through representation, it’s undeniable,” says Artiges. “Otherwise media moguls such as Rupert Murdoch and Vincent Bolloré would not devote so much effort to shaping public opinion… What surprises me is that, despite the many examples of abuse, failure, and the arbitrariness that often accompanies it, power itself is not being challenged more seriously. It no longer seems implausible that Donald Trump might refuse to leave office at the end of his second term; the man who performed a fascist salute at his inauguration remains the richest person on Earth.

“There are voters in France who sincerely believe a 30-year-old man represents the solution to their problems. Today his name is Bardella; yesterday it was Macron. And even though their ideas are not equivalent, their political projects differ, the hope, fervour and even adoration they inspire are remarkably similar.”
