item.title: Jaou Tunis Biennale returns with newly-commissioned work - 1854 Photography
item.description:
Image © Sara Kontar

Featuring newly-commissioned projects, Jaou Tunis Biennale is a major focal point for visual arts from the Global South and its diaspora, open from 23 October-22 November in the Tunisian capital then touring internationally 

This October, the lens-based art world shifts its gaze toward North Africa as the 8th edition of the Jaou Tunis Biennale once again transforms the Tunisian capital. Running from 23 October to 22 November,  the month-long festival arrives as a highly-anticipated focal point for global and diasporic visual culture, turning the historic city into what organisers describe as a “biennale-archipel” – an interconnected network of ideas, images, and geographies.

Founded in 2013 by the Kamel Lazaar Foundation, Jaou Tunis Biennale has long championed artists and lens-based practices from the Global Majority, bridging the Mediterranean to challenge eurocentric art narratives. This year marks a pivotal  milestone for the bi-yearly event; for the first time in its history, Geneva’s prestigious Biennale de l’Image en Mouvement (BIM’26) leaves Switzerland to debut in the African continent. The Art Explora Foundation’s nomadic Mediterranean festival will also conclude its journey across the sea, anchoring its final destination in the heart of Tunis.

Co-curated by Lina Lazaar and Andrea Bellini, the centrepiece of this collaborative edition is the exhibition Becoming the Ocean. Housed inside the Quechlet El Attarine – a 19th-century Ottoman military barracks nestled within the UNESCO-listed Medina – the show draws inspiration from Khalil Gibran’s metaphor of a river that mistakes transformation for disappearance, reflecting on a world in which inherited structures are increasingly unable to respond to the crises they have produced. 

Rather than asking how to preserve a world already slipping away, Becoming the Ocean asks which new iterations of memory and solidarity appear when we recognise that survival is dependent on interconnectedness, not independence. Featuring 16 newly-commissioned works from an international cohort of emerging and established artists across Africa, the Arab world, Latin America, and Asia, the exhibition builds a strong platform for female and MENA-region perspectives. Prominent participating names include Tabarak Allah Abbas, Hajra Waheed, Sarah Zeryab, and Younès Ben Slimane. Among the many exciting emerging artists exhibiting are Alaa Mansour, Liv Schulman, and Castiel Vitorino Brasileiro. 

Through the malleability of the moving image, these artists confront critical systemic transitions, memory preservation, and alternative responses to societal crises. True to its colloquial Tunisian name – “Jaou“ loosely translates to “atmosphere” or  “good vibes” – the biennale refuses to stay confined within traditional white cube gallery spaces. Rather, it roams free and becomes intertwined with the fabric of the city itself. Beyond the central military barracks, photography installations, audio-visual environments, and live performances are set in iconic local markers, including the Église Sainte-Croix, Cinema Rio, the Ancienne Bourse du Travail, and the B7L9 Art Centre.

Complementing the core moving-image exhibition, an eclectic public programme will offer dedicated photography workshops for emerging talent, site-specific performances, and an international symposium addressing the future of Mediterranean cultural cross-pollination. BJP is also partnering up with British Council, to run a portfolio review on 26 October which starts at 2pm. Becoming the Ocean ventures beyond art installations too, with some of the exhibiting artists also joining panels to consider their work and their role within and responsibility towards their chosen medium and the world at large. Guest speakers include Mohammed el-Kurd and Shimon Basar.

Following its initial presentation in Tunis, Becoming the Ocean is slated to tour major art capitals including Venice, Brussels, Geneva and London (at Ibraaz), giving these newly-commissioned projects an international reach. For audiences looking to discover a glimpse of  the visual arts  from the Global South and its diaspora, Jaou Tunis 2026 promises an original, urgent, and deeply communal space. BJP will be sharing stories and highlights from Jaou Tunis as it unfolds.

Jaou Tunis Biennale is open from 23 October – 22 November https://jaou.tn

item.title: Paris Photo 2026 celebrates 200 years of photography - 1854 Photography
item.description:
jpeg ib02, 2007 © Thomas Ruff/Artists Rights Society (ARS). Courtesy of New York/VG Bild-Kunst, Germany.

As France marks the bicentennial of photography, Paris Photo considers the history and future of a constantly evolving medium

When was photography invented? France is drawing a line in the sand at 1827 when, between 04 June and 18 July, Nicéphore Niépce fixed an image of the view from a window in his country estate. The nation is celebrating the bicentennial from September 2026 to September 2027 and the first major event in the calendar is Paris Photo; the history and technology of image-making will thread through the fair. “Paris Photo presents a panorama of photography, from the 19th century to the latest experimentations with digital art. This year even more, we will highlight the diversity of photography practices through 200 years of history,” says Florence Bourgeois, director of Paris Photo. “There will be a focus on the historical thread of the medium.”

The fair will feature a retrospective by Thomas Ruff, a contemporary artist renown for his work investigating the nature and technology of photography; his installation will include works from Sterne (‘Stars’, 1989–1992), made with images from the European Southern Observatory, and from Jpegs (2004–2009), pixelated images of landscapes, modern technology and historical events. Florian Ebner and Damarice Amao, from the Centre Pompidou/Musée National d’Art Moderne, have been invited to curate a show on the development of photography, meanwhile, drawing on the institution’s collection with Julie Jones, director of the Maison Européenne de la Photographie. And the booths will include more galleries presenting prints from the early years of image-making. 

“We look at the history of photography from a contemporary point of view,” explains Anna Planas, artistic director of Paris Photo. “To mark the bicentenary, our entrance statement will be dedicated to the work of Thomas Ruff, across a wall of nearly 40 meters long at the entrance of the Grand Palais. The installation will highlight Ruff’s engagement with the medium and its evolving technologies offering an exploration of the grammar of photography.”

“This year we will welcome galleries and publishers from 38 countries – the fair is becoming more and more open” – Anna Planas

Other presentations will also consider photography as a medium. Galerie Christophe Gaillard is bringing a solo display by Isabelle Le Minh, for example, a contemporary artist who highlights the new properties of digital images; London’s Large Glass “will confront historical work with contemporary in a show where each artist is paired with a historical figure, connected by places of significance or shared themes,” says Planas. The Voices sector, which is curated by Francesco Zanot and Zasha Colah and dedicated to contemporary image-makers, will explore an emerging paradox – conceived as a tool to preserve that which would otherwise vanish, photography is being celebrated just as its traditional form appears unstable, transformed and challenged by processes altering its nature and status.

Titled La Disparition (‘The Disappearance’), Voices will include work by Léonard Pongo, a Belgian-Congolese artist who plays with the limits of visibility. Pongo’s work was presented in the 2026 Venice Biennale and, says Planas, the 2026 Voices curators bring insight into both photography and the contemporary art landscape. “Francesco is a photography curator and researcher,” she explains. “Zasha comes from the contemporary art world. This is something we also really enjoy, opening up to curators from outside photography.”

The Digital sector will be curated by Marco De Mutiis, digital curator at Fotomuseum Winterthur in Switzerland, and editor of the 2025 publication The Lure of the Image. Bringing the medium up to the present day, his selection also draws on a longer history of photography and of digital imaging. “Photography has been a continuously unstable, constantly changing medium,” he says. “And digital has fundamentally transformed it. But there is also a specificity of the image that has formed how we see the world. The Digital sector will include artists who show how photography has changed, from glitches and Photoshop to AI and machine learning, but we will also consider that ongoing history.”

Photography’s roots are in science, positivism and the drive for efficiency, he adds, “and we should always remember that the camera was invented in the time of the Industrial Revolution, a time of an ideology which was powerful in erasing other forms, and which still lies at the root of many neoliberal societies”. But there is also an alternative history of photographs linked with spiritualism, ghosts and the occult, he argues, more esoteric beliefs which are somehow resurfacing now. 

“I have been interested to see many artists now coming back to magic, perhaps as a way to escape the algorithm,” he says. “This algorithm seems to be dictating our lives, so forms that are subjective or embrace mystery and even magic are an escape from that, almost a refuge or resistance to this scientific eye.”

Elsewhere at Paris Photo other alternative histories will also be traced. An association of Argentinian galleries will show how photography developed in the country, for example, with Rolf Art presenting innovative artist Adriana Lestido, and Vasari bringing a group show – after last year devoting its booth to Julio Le Parc, the groundbreaking op artist now showing a major retrospective at Tate Modern. 

The Emergence sector will include Randa Mirza, who photographs the south of Lebanon, and shows the destruction caused by Israeli attacks; it will also feature Nicolás Combarro, whose work considers concentration camps and how to depict them, in the absence of historical images. Over in the talks programme, Tina Campt, professor of humanities at Princeton University and author of books such as Listening to Images, and A Black Gaze: Artists Changing How We See, will be in-conversation with South African visual activist and photographer Zanele Muholi. 

“We trigger as much diversity as possible,” says Planas. “This year we will welcome galleries and publishers from 38 countries – the fair is becoming more and more open, and the bicentenary may also have an attractive effect to the international community.”

“Through our conversation and book talks programmes, curated paths and specific presentations, we have the will to give a wide vision of photography today,” adds Bourgeois.

Paris Photo takes place from 12-15 November 2026 at the Grand Palais.

item.title: Nikita Teryoshin and the imagery of protest, artwashing and political defiance with Pussy Riot - 1854 Photography
item.description:
Not in My Name © Nikita Teryoshin.

Invited to document feminist performance art collective Pussy Riot protesting the Russian Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, Nikita Teryoshin became part of the action in the wider world

In early 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russian-born photographer Nikita Teryoshin was commissioned by a German news magazine to document the influx of Ukrainian refugees across the Polish border. Due to a hand injury, he was forced to pull out of the job, and was left feeling listless. Long estranged from his country of birth, and horrified by the events that were unfolding on Europe’s eastern border, he felt the urge to use his camera to make a statement. So taking his Russian passport, he held it against a grey Berlin sky, set it on fire, and photographed it. 

Born in Leningrad, Teryoshin moved to Dortmund, Germany, as a teenager. His father worked as a set designer and painter for theatre and television, and the young Nikita found these studios and workshops fascinating. It was perhaps there he developed a certain sensitivity to the construction of images, the way that arrangements of objects, bodies and lighting create meaning, and the technical tricks and special effects that can confuse an audience’s sense of the real. From there he realised that, across culture, media and politics, there is almost always a ‘backstage’, a hidden space in which spectacle is carefully engineered, labour is invisibilised, and wealth and reputation are laundered. 

Teryoshin’s personal projects have since explored the global arms trade and the marketing of war, political conventions and the apparatus of governance, and the strategies of artwashing and sportswashing employed by repressive kleptocracies. Around the time he burned his Russian passport, he was part of a burgeoning online NFT community, through which he engaged with many Ukrainian and Russian artists. “It was super supportive,” he says. “Photographers from all over the world, helping each other out. I thought, maybe I can mint this photo of my passport, and raise some money for Ukraine.” 

He minted and sold the NFT, and printed posters and limited editions of the image, raising thousands of euros which he donated to causes in Ukraine. The photograph was published in German broadsheet Die Zeit, and circulated widely online. Some Russians mocked the burning as cowardly and superficial, enacted from the relative safety of a third nation. An old classmate of Teryoshin’s posted on social media that she had reported the image to security services and that, if he attempted to return to Russia, he would be escorted directly from the plane to a prison cell. 

Teryoshin is sanguine. “From the beginning, it was pretty clear that I can’t go back [to Russia],” he says. “Before the full-scale invasion, burning a passport would have landed you with a fine. But they’ve changed the law, and applied it retrospectively, so it’s now 16 years in prison.”

“It’s absurd to say that you’re not into politics and you’re against the war, but then be comfortable going out onto a global stage and representing [the aggressor]” – Nikita Teryoshin

The photographic medium is deeply implicated in the ecologies of contemporary protest. Setting fire to passports, flags and sacred texts as an act of resistance relies on the presence of a camera for political potency and endurance. Photographs of flames seem to arrest the physics of combustion, and suggest that a fire might, in fact, burn ceaselessly. The image of Teryoshin’s flaming passport is a performance of ritualised agency that lingers conceptually, with the potential to act as a universal igniting force. And the idea that a political fire could burn forever in the hearts and minds of a population is the kind of notion that tends to trouble insecure autocrats. 

After the death of Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny in a Siberian penal colony in February 2024, Teryoshin joined a protest at Berlin’s Russian embassy, organised by the dissident feminist performance art collective Pussy Riot. Taking some photographs, he sent them to the group afterwards. Two years later – after a disorienting visit to Qatar to shoot the petrostate’s inaugural edition of the prestigious commercial art fair Art Basel – Teryoshin was reflecting on how the art world functions as a geopolitical instrument for intersecting spheres of power and conflict. Then he received a message from Pussy Riot’s founding member, Nadya Tolokonnikova; the group would be staging a protest outside the Russian Pavilion during the preview week of the Venice Biennale, and they wanted him to document it. It seemed to Teryoshin like “a greeting from the universe”.

Since their formation in 2011, Pussy Riot have adopted strategies of punk spectacle and aesthetic actionism, producing pictorially intense and vivid image-acts that seem to prioritise the visual afterlife of protest over the act itself. The group emerged at around the same time as Instagram, a time when everyone from the Pope to the Israel Defense Forces was joining Twitter, and when social networks were having far-reaching off-screen sociopolitical impact (including during the Arab Spring). Highly digitally literate, and well aware of the political power of their (youthful, female) bodies as a form of media, Pussy Riot typically brief photographers and bloggers in advance of their upcoming actions. 

Image production is a key component of their strategy, the group adopting hybridised radical feminist approaches to protest to explore the argumentative potential of visibility. Their brightly coloured balaclavas are an important visual motif within this strategy, and they anonymise and de-individualise group members. Pussy Riot have claimed to have dozens of members, and say that their participants can totally differ in each guerilla performance. Their headwear also creates visual parallels with other direct action, liberation and feminist movements, which have embraced the balaclava as a performative object.

The presence of Femen, which was founded in Ukraine but now operates internationally, adds a further dimension. Femen employ their own naked bodies as a form of media, forcing a confrontation with the precarity and vulnerability of the nude female form – and crucially, generating further visibility. With slogans painted across their bare breasts, Femen attempt to invert the hypersexualised connotations of female anatomy, and suggest that the body can assert its own meanings and values. 

It is a strategy that has been critiqued. What Femen present as a liberated female image has been criticised as a hegemonically white, thin and able-bodied representation; the group has also been accused of prioritising a deeply Western view of female emancipation, specifically targeting Islam and rejecting women who have an alternative relationship with their bodies. Femen activists’ confrontations with law enforcement and security services make for compelling imagery, but the political meanings they produce are not always shared. 

Nevertheless, as Judith Butler writes in Notes Toward a Performative Theory of Assembly, “though the body in its struggle with precarity and persistence is at the heart of so many demonstrations, it is also the body that is on the line, exhibiting its value and its freedom in the demonstration itself, enacting, by the embodied form of the gathering, a claim to the political”. Pussy Riot and Femen’s emphasis on corporeality risks reinforcing the patriarchal notion that the attention paid to women should be arbitrated by their physical appearance. However, it is worth remembering that in the Russian and post-Soviet cultural context, in which the Orthodox Church wields significant influence, the presence of non-conforming female bodies in public space can still be considered societally menacing. 

“Russia wages hybrid war,” explained Tolokonnikova to the assembled press on the steps of the Russian Pavilion, as the protest was dissipating. “It’s not just tanks and drones, murders and rapes in Ukraine, but it’s also culture, art, language, so called ‘soft power’. It’s clear that it’s part of their military strategy and that’s the way they try and conquer the West. And you guys just open the doors to them,” she continued, before concluding with a weary sarcasm: “That’s funny.” 

When challenged on the presence of states accused of crimes against humanity, Biennale president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco appealed to liberal false balance; “If the Biennale started selecting works [on the basis of] passports, it would cease to be what it has always been: the place where the world comes together.” It seems a platitudinal take from the conservative intellectual – and former leader of the youth wing of the neo-fascist Italian Social Movement party – confusing rogue state propaganda with artistic freedom. 

Teryoshin is alive to the paradox that emerges when “the world comes together” in Venice. “I think the normalisation of Russia’s presence in Europe, in this cultural environment, is totally wrong,” he states. “People say to me, ‘Yeah, but the artists who are part of it are not into politics’. Or, ‘There is no one from Russia who is really into this war’. But it’s absurd to say that you’re not into politics and you’re against the war, but then be comfortable going out onto a global stage and representing [the aggressor]. One of the best examples of artwashing is this pavilion.” 

He accepts his position as an active agent in the protest’s efficacy – especially as the Russian Pavilion was only open during preview week, when few members of the public would have been present for the demonstration. “You could say the photographs become more important than the action itself,” Teryoshin reflects. “There were maybe 200 people there at that moment. But the only thing the world will see are the pictures.”

item.title: Dreamy work by SWANA artists on show in Perth - 1854 Photography
item.description:
From What’s Ours. Lebanon. 2013-2023 © Myriam Boulos. Courtesy of the artist

Gathering work by seven living artists and one artist duo from across South West Asia, North Africa, and its many diasporas, No night is long enough for us to dream twice presents an expanded approach to image-making at the Art Gallery of Western Australia

“No night is long enough for us to dream twice” is a celebrated line from the poem The Raven’s Ink, by Palestinian author Mahmoud Darwish. Born in al-Birwa in 1941, Darwish was forced to flee the village with his family in 1948, when it was captured and razed by the Israel Defense Forces; the family managed to return to close nearby but, having missed the Israeli census, was assigned ‘present-absent aliens’. Darwish found this situation absurd, and he used absurdism and surrealism in his poems to articulate the fragmented reality of exile. But he also used them to envisage new possibilities. His poems are “lyrical, imagistic, plaintive, haunting, always passionate and elegant – and never anything less than free – what he would dream for all his people”, poet Naomi Shihab Nye has said. 

Curator Dalia Al-Dujaili was inspired by Darwish’s practice when working on the exhibition No night is long enough for us to dream twice, on show at The Art Gallery of Western Australia until 31 January; putting together work by artists from across the SWANA region and its diaspora with co-curator Rachel Cieśla, she wanted to reach beyond the documentary imagery so often seen from this area, and towards something more liberatory. “I was curious to explore how regional and diaspora SWANA artists utilise artistic movements and philosophical approaches such as absurdism and surrealism to expand the possibility of photography,” she explains. “So much of the work from our region is stuck in war or documentary aesthetics and approaches, and whilst useful in some contexts, it feels flattening, dehumanising and also limiting for the artistic careers of these photographers. 

“I also feel like Eurocentric curatorial approaches impose these kinds of aesthetics and want to go to shows about the SWANA expecting a certain kind of mood or vision, which I really wanted to challenge. I was not interested in flags and pomegranates and these heroic images of liberation – though, again, so beautiful in other contexts. I wanted audiences to be surprised by the universality of concepts like play, desire, lust, violence and celebration and how these play out in the region when they are scrutinised under the camera lens.”

“The idea I’ve been working with is ‘documentary futurity’: a documentary impulse that records what is happening while also imagining what could come next,” adds Cieśla. “Dreaming is the right word for that, because a dream isn’t a record of the past. It’s the mind opening out onto another world that I’ve created in order to try out another possibility. In the exhibition, you see photographs and videos that stay with difficult sites without settling into elegy. They keep a door open.”

“The idea I’ve been working with is ‘documentary futurity’: a documentary impulse that records what is happening while also imagining what could come next.” Rachel Cieśla

No night is long enough for us to dream twice includes seven living artists and one artist duo whose work opens this sense of possibility; the artists span the South West Asia North Africa region, including Algeria, Iran, Lebanon, Morocco, Palestine, and Türkiye. The exhibition includes a site-specific new iteration of Abdulhamid Kircher’s Rotting from within (2026), which includes photographs, family snaps, and 30 video works to create a dense collage, seemingly at the edge of what it can contain. Describing Kircher’s relationship with his estranged father, Rotting from within includes moments of peace and love, all the joy and pain of what the curators describe as “the unruly complexity of lived experience”. 

Lebanese image-maker Mohamad Abdouni considers family alongside intimacy and queer experience, in which images become inseparable from questions of belonging and visibility; Hicham Benohoud – who hails from a different generation – embraces a different kind of messy with his portraits of Moroccan school children, taken while he was an art teacher. Disillusioned with the rigid four-hour lessons he was expected to run, Benohoud transformed his classroom into a studio in which the students could be creatively free. Photographing the results between 1994-2002, his images are warm and anarchic; they also imply a critique of the education system, and what Benohoud saw as its failings.

Sabiha Çimen explores life for school kids too, her series Hafiz shot in girls-only Qur’an schools in Turkey; finding moments of humour and intimacy, it speaks of rich inner lives inside the uniforms. Born in Istanbul, Çimen is a self-taught photographer and now a member of Magnum Photos; Hafiz was her first photobook, and it won the 2022 Paris Photo-Aperture First PhotoBook award. No night is long enough for us to dream twice also includes important projects by Myriam Boulos and Hannah Darabi, both of whom explore intimacy and sexuality amid times of protest and political change; Boulos is from Lebanon, and is also a member of Magnum Photos, while Darabi uses found images to talk of Iran. Darabi’s Why Don’t You Dance? used collage as a means to discuss bodily autonomy and personal liberation; No night is long enough for us to dream twice includes a satirical 1980s gym dance class, which Darabi shot as a video work.

The exhibition also includes two other video works. Basel Abbas and Ruanne Abou-Rahme, who are of Palestinian descent, contribute the video-sound installation Collapse, which combines original documentary and material from historic films and “leads you into the slightly darker moments of the show”; Mohamed Bourouissa, the Algerian-born French photographer, shows his video work Généalogie de la Violence (Genealogy of Violence), 2024, in which a young couple in a car chat and discuss their future – until they are interrupted by a police identity check. Bourouissa is also exhibiting his seminal image Le cercle imaginaire (2007-08), from broader work Périphérique, which investigates social tensions in the marginalised Parisian banlieues.

Darabi’s film is being shown on an appropriately retro 1980s TV, but the two other films are being shown at large scale, as are many of the images, and Kircher’s whole-wall installation. “We blew a lot of the images up because we wanted the show to feel really immersive,” Al-Dujaili explains. “I talk about it like walking through a fever dream.” She and Cieśla have also included a book display to help add context though; the audience in Perth won’t necessarily have much knowledge or understanding of the richness of SWANA-region photography, Al-Dujaili points out, so they wanted to help them get acquainted. “It felt important to challenge what these audiences might expect walking into a SWANA show, and hopefully they will leave with a new ‘to read’ list or a new photobook in their hands.”

And it was books that brought Al-Dujaili and Cieśla together, and helped bring the show into being; Cieśla heard about Al-Dujaili through her HIKMA project – an online repository and library for materials on Mesopotamia and modern day Iraq – and reached out to her via WhatsApp. Their shared interest in photography from the SWANA region and its diaspora soon became clear, and evolved into the idea of an exhibition around this work and the theme of dreams. Cieśla is Lead Creative at The Simon Lee Foundation Institute of Contemporary Asian Art, a curatorial initiative at The Art Gallery of Western Australia which she describes as “working to enrich AGWA’s connections with contemporary artists and cultural thinking in Asia and across its diasporas”. The Institute is wary of shows that are geographically bounded in a fixed sense, she adds, so No night is long enough for us to dream twice is deliberately wide, including artists from across the region and its diaspora rather than honing in on a particular culture. 

This approach is also appropriate, she adds, reflecting its geographical, political and cultural history. “The borders across SWANA have been drawn and redrawn, and people move across them constantly, through exile, migration and family ties. A show built around one place might have treated those lines as fixed, when for many of these artists they aren’t. It also meant we could include artists working in the diaspora, whose images are shaped by distance as much as by where they come from. What we were drawn to instead was something these artists share beyond a common geography – a relation to pressure,” she continues. “Each of them makes images within spaces where social forces are building, breaking and building again, whether that’s a city, a home, or a body. Putting them side-by-side lets you see how that pressure shows up differently in each context, and what echoes between them anyway.”

No night is long enough for us to dream twice is on show at The Art Gallery of Western Australia until 31 January 2027 artgallery.wa.gov.au

item.title: Aga Łuczakowska offers a quiet meditation on Ceaușescu’s legacy in Bucharest - 1854 Photography
item.description:
Image from Râsu’-plânsu’ © Aga Łuczakowska.

Moments of sensitivity and symbolism in the everyday environment infuse Łuczakowska’s self-published book, Râsu’-plânsu’.

The Romanian phrase râsu’-plânsu’ (‘laughing through tears’) describes the ability to discover moments of tenderness, irony and resilience within hardship. In Aga Łuczakowska’s beautifully produced 60-page softback, the phrase becomes less historical explanation and more invitation – a brief, immersive encounter with a different way of reading place, memory and the traces people leave behind.

Rather than offering an exhaustive account of former president Nicolae Ceaușescu’s dictatorial programme of forced relocation and urbanisation, Râsu’-plânsu’ operates as a poetic meditation. Across a decade living in Bucharest, Łuczakowska photographed fragments of the city on her way to work and during weekends, allowing the rhythm of everyday life to reveal the quiet contradictions embedded within the built environment.

Her black-and-white images look beyond the imposing concrete structures of the dictatorship’s housing estates to uncover the persistence of older memories and personal histories. A seemingly cheap floral blanket hanging from a washing line becomes a quietly profound image, the chintzy pattern carrying echoes of folk tradition and a rural imagination within the stark geometry of brutalist modernity. Elsewhere repeated fragments of domestic bric-a-brac appear, boxes, broken metalwork, objects that feel both lost and preserved, brittle yet enduring.

Râsu’-plânsu’ asks the viewer to slow down and look differently. Its power comes not from scale or completeness, but from the intimacy of its observations

Łuczakowska’s work excels in its sensitivity to these small, almost imperceptible signals. She photographs not simply what is present but evidence of adaptation within an imposed architectural order. A quiet, understated book, Râsu’-plânsu’ asks the viewer to slow down and look differently. Its power comes not from scale or completeness, but from the intimacy of its observations, which reveal how memory, identity and human resilience persist within spaces designed to transform them. 

In a neat twist on the basic premise, Łuczakowska has also asked artists to adapt her publication, inviting them to add drawings or pages, or cut into existing images. Allowing the project to expand beyond her authorship, she has named this ongoing project Râsu’-plânsu’ Interventions, embracing a decentralisation of power – an anti-authoritarianism – that even extends to her own work.

Râsu’-plânsu’ by Aga Łuczakowska is self-published, priced €30.

item.title: Tate Modern explores the history of pictorialism in major exhibition - 1854 Photography
item.description:
Doble perfil, 1942 © Annemarie Heinrich/Estate of the artist.

Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography, a new exhibition at Tate Modern, showcases the history of pictorialism and how it expanded the possibilities of photography as an art form

A serene landscape showing splashing white ducks who seem to merge seamlessly with the babbling water, shadowy trees looming like dark mountains. This photograph, part of Tate Modern’s exhibition Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography, was taken by Liu Bannong in 1927 after the Chinese photographer returned from studying linguistics in Paris, where pictorialism was pursued by artists running their own salons, and publishing magazines on art photography. Pictorialism was the first move towards proclaiming photography an art form yet, until now, its impact on image-making practice in south-east and south Asia has been relatively unknown. The Tate’s exhibition fills these lacunae by looking at this movement as transcontinental.

Pictorialism was initially theorised by English photographer Henry Peach Robinson, whose 1869 instructional book Pictorial Effect in Photography urged image-makers to follow the order and composition in painting, rather than simply documenting reality. Armed with such influences Bannong produced a text of his own – Bannong tanying (‘Bannong’s Comments on Photography’) – which drew from the aesthetic discourse of traditional Chinese painting. It argued for photography as an expressive medium revealing an inner world of emotion. This dialogue was continued by others, including Long Chin-San, whose essay Photography and Chinese Painting (1955) advised ‘choosing’ the good parts of a photograph, emulating the approach of traditional Chinese art.

“Contemporary photographic art is where it is today due to the efforts by pictorialists to carve out a space for photography within fine art” – Charmaine Toh, curator

The ‘selection’ Chin-San referred to is seen in Singaporean Lee Sow Lim’s early work, which uses layers of photo negatives to arrive at a single image. Transferring an ethereal quality from Chinese ink paintings into photographic imagery, Sow Lim even stamped the results with a traditional painterly red seal. His later works are abstractions in colour – Singaporean artist Tan Lip Seng’s works were figurative but, created with layers of high contrast and highly saturated colour transparencies, were equally innovative. Not all pictorialists were in favour of manipulated images. British writer and photographer PH Emerson favoured naturalism, controlling light and composition to create beauty – as did Singaporean Yip Cheong Fun, in his portraits of fishermen and children. 

None of this was happening in isolation, but within photo clubs and salons in south-east and south Asia with an interest in pictorialism that continued long after modernist photography had taken over in the West. Many camera clubs had initially started as forums for colonial officials and local amateur photographers, building information for British administrators; Photographic Societies of Bombay (1854) and Bengal (1856) conducted ethnographic studies, for example. But, points out Charmaine Toh, senior curator of international art (photography) at the Tate and curator of the Tate Modern show, “these clubs started at a time when most of south-east Asia was on the verge of independence”, and pictorialism for many offered a deviation from the surveying gaze. It also allowed the opportunity to showcase worldwide as these salons had access to journals with details for open calls.

While pictorialism changed the language of ethnographic photography in Elli Sougioultzoglou-Seraidari’s images of refugees in Attica in the mid-1920s, it also allowed photographers in the colonies alternative approaches to self-representation. They set up other societies, such as the Photographic Society of India (1937), co-founded by mill-worker Dhirajlal R Mody, or the Photographic Society of Ceylon (1935) by Sri Lankan photographer Lionel Wendt. Wendt’s portraits of the male body in the 1930s and early 1940s introduced fluidity and homoeroticism, depicting men far beyond their castes and professions. The images departed from the buttoned-up ethnographic representations – though Toh warns against drawing easy conclusions, pointing out that the body was still performing in Wendt’s work, re-rehearsing privileged stereotypes.

“Some photographers would continue using colonial ‘tropes’, like photographing someone in a sarong in Malaysia, to get accepted into exhibitions overseas,” explains Toh. “It was a certain agency as they played up to Western expectations and then won awards at international salons. This was important to see themselves as entering a new era of postcolonial modernity.” Wendt sent his works to London or Paris, the colonial centres at the time; even so, his works and images by others have not been included in the history of pictorialism. 

“Piecing together this history is on-ground work and opening boxes,” says Toh, whose research included meeting with photographers’ families to find long-lost archives and prints. “The RPS Collection became a major resource as these photographers would send their prints to London for the RPS annual exhibition – and didn’t ask for them back,” she adds. “Behind these prints is an entire history of where it has travelled to, even between countries who weren’t getting along diplomatically.”

And, while pictorialism arguably never went away, contemporary preoccupations with the ideology of a certain photographic gaze, or with questioning the medium more generally, owe much to these predecessors. “Contemporary photographic art is where it is today due to the efforts by pictorialists to carve out a space for photography within fine art,” reflects Toh.

Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography is at Tate Modern, London, until 21 February 2027.

item.title: Sanlé Sory’s colour work comes to The Photographers’ Gallery - 1854 Photography
item.description:
All images © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta. Sanlé Sory photographed at Volta Photo Studio in Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso.

The Burkina Faso artist’s later work reveals the changing ethos and sociopolitical shifts in West African photography

When asked why The Photographers’ Gallery is displaying later colour works by the Burkinabe studio photographer Sanlé Sory – and why now – TPG curator Taous Dahmani’s answer is clear and direct: “Because I’m here now.”

“I had always wanted to think about the long tradition of West African studio photography as a global surface,” she adds. Fed up with dominant readings, Dahmani argues that these photographs require a relocation of function if they are to be understood in more generative, restorative ways. The job of photographer is political, artistic, often polemic and gestural; it is also, fundamentally, a job. It is labour. It is a means to get paid and a way to live one’s life, void of a punch card and with freedom to roam. Photography is a history of grafting, of making ends meet, of waking up and going to work. Dahmani looks away from the recent landscape of “revived” West African photographic exhibitions, literally blown up for the Western art powers that be, and instead sees them as they are: small and intimate. And that is enough. 

Perhaps ‘fine art’ – whatever that means – is a poisoned chalice, a trapdoored pedestal, a gilded cage. Instead, Sory is here a master craftsman, but one looking to get paid rather than necessarily disrupt the canon. This curse of fine art, which fixes Sory’s oeuvre and character into something discovered, demanding recontextualisation, and subsequent elevation, in turn shuts a door into the modern world.

“[Sory’s later colour work] holds quite a significant shift in what we know about the history of West African practice” – Taous Dahmani, curator

Reductive readings often position this sort of photographer, and by extent photography, as a historical event over a living being. Dahmani says this limited reading “refuses entry into contemporality”, and perpetuates Western art narratives as “acceptable forms of nostalgia about this past of liberation, a call to the time ‘when we liberated poor Africans’”. On the two far sides of the Atlantic, and deep in the white cube, when we see West African studio portraits, it is always revolutionary times. Nothing ever changes, Africa is Africa, and the West is the West. 

But Sory’s archive holds “thousands and thousands” of later colour negatives, many of which have never been printed beyond their original commission. Dahmani asks why and steers towards a relocation, a “re-anchoring” in her terms. Perhaps these colour works, a move on from the earlier black-and-white work of the 1960s and 70s, were deemed harder to digest for Western audiences, something less fixed than the story we know (or have been told). To Dahmani, Burkina Faso, and the wider African stage, is not a fixed event but a site to examine universal photographic systems, alongside the specificities of 20th-century African histories. “[Sory’s later colour work] holds quite a significant shift in what we know about the history of West African practice,” she says. 

She reads the practice as both ubiquitous and unique; closer to the functional, political and social histories caught within the portraits, and understood as wholly commissioned artefacts. Yet by curating the show in London there is an awareness that home is not always a place one can return to, that there is perhaps no true contextual providence left. Instead there is a possibility to seek out new lands, ways of being and seeing, ones which bring the photographs to audiences new and old, but allow all those looking to see for themselves. 

The Western art reading has a tendency to turn African nations into islands, dislocating them from neighbouring, concurrent histories. Dahmani refers to this as a “dictated, fetishised history”, one the market embraces with ease but which brings us no closer to understanding these images or people. “For me, colour became the starting point,” she says. “Can we think critically about this history through the lens of colour? Can we think of it as a form of politics? Most of the pictures we know are from the 1960s and 70s. Postcolonial moments of aspiration, of joy… at least that’s how it’s sold. Moments of ‘Finally, the freedom of the African people!’ But it stops there. No one wonders what happens after.”

Sory’s later portraits of street vendors, personable and direct, grew out of a slowing appetite for commissioned portraits. Cameraphones had arrived and times were changing. Dahmani also stresses the desires of the later sitters he was commissioned to record, commenting on their input into the images. “Sory printed in black-and-white, but when colour became more accessible, clients asked for it. It was more expensive, and he suddenly couldn’t work alone.” For Dahmani, both sitter and printer become producer and collaborator.  

Dahmani traces stories of the sitters through historical relocations; every now and then you notice someone dressed fancifully for the camera, who is “wearing a suit slightly too small, their shoes maybe unvarnished”. Through these images Dahmani moves away from a fashion-first reading towards something more akin to socially informed style studies, an analysis of hand-me-downs and counterfeit designerwear. This becomes part of the re-anchoring, and perhaps a new type of non-hierarchical photographic kinship. It aids an understanding of universality, not exotic idiosyncrasy, though a story that is also deeply African. 

Sory had to negotiate and barter with his subjects, as ultimately the images existed off their payments. He had to follow trends, keep up with the changing times. Suddenly people did not want his famed illustrated backdrops any longer. “They wanted to be part of a new technology, and a new capacity of being seen,” Dahmani explains. Sory, as with many West African portraitists, is rarely discussed within the contexts of an emerging contemporary. Entry into the modern world, with colour, Nike, Obama T-shirts, and iPhones, has not been curatorially permitted.

“I now don’t have to prove that photography is an art form,” Dahmani states. “But I do want to get back to the fact that actually, historically, there were things that we were too quick to put into one category, instead of allowing them to be a multiplicity of things. And I don’t think we often allow African artists to be a multiplicity of things.”

Sanlé Sory: Colour Years is at The Photographers’ Gallery,  London, from 14 October 2026 to 21 February 2027. The accompanying book is published by GOST, priced £45 https://gostbooks.com/products/volta-colour

item.title: Last chance to see Kyotographie: Kawada Kikuji x Iwane Ai - 1854 Photography
item.description:
From the series A New River © Iwane Ai

Moving work by artists from two generations is evocatively installed at Japan House

In London for Frieze? Luckily you can still see Kyotographie: Kawada Kikuji x Iwane Ai, on show at Japan House London until 18 October. Organised by the celebrated Japanese photography festival, the exhibition brings together two image-makers whose work resonates with shared concerns about how we place ourselves in the world, how we travel through life, and how photography can represent both. 

Kawada presents works from the 1950s until today, including his series Chizu (The Map); published as a book in 1965, exactly 20 years after the US dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, it records munitions bunkers, Special Forces soldiers, and survivors with facial scars. It also shows Lucky Strike cigarettes and Coca-Cola bottles, American consumer goods Kawada found in the wrecked city.

Kawada came to prominence in the 1960s, after founding the VIVO collective with image-makers such as Eikoh Hosoe and Shōmei Tōmatsu; eschewing the quasi-objective documentary photograph they embraced an “are-bure-boke” – “blurry and out-of-focus” – approach that evoked a deeper reality. “I don’t start out with a title or theme in mind,” Kawada says in a video made with Kyotographie. “But then suddenly, unexpectedly, something really not logically, but intuitively, appears out of nowhere. That’s how it works.”

His installation also includes a projection room, flicking through shots he recently posted on Instagram; Kawada continues to play with his medium, still restlessly experimental though he’s now nearing 100 years old. “Since photography inevitably cuts out a single moment, that also means you can reconstruct time in any way you like,” he says. “When various layers of time overlap, then human psychology, the atmosphere of an era, the state of society, even my own mental state – all these emerge. That’s why I always take this approach.”

“I don’t start out with a title or theme in mind. But then suddenly, unexpectedly, something really not logically, but intuitively, appears out of nowhere.” Kawada Kikuji

Born in 1975, Iwane is from a different generation yet testing limits runs through her practice too. She’s showing a work titled Kipuka, which she shot in 2018; focusing on Japanese immigrant communities in Hawaii, it centres on the o-bon, a festival for honouring the ancestors and the dead. The festival includes a circular dance, and a particular song, the ‘Fukushima Ondo’, originally from the area devastated by the 2011 earthquake, tsunami, and nuclear accident.

Using a rotating panoramic camera – traditionally used by these communities to photograph funerals – Iwane gathers the many individuals at the festival, and displays the resulting long prints as curling walkways. The visitor must walk in between, immersing themselves in the crowd. Her images also include panoramic shots of cemeteries, and of the destruction wrought on quiet streets, by a nature that’s beyond human control.

Iwane is also showing her series A New River, shot during the Covid pandemic in 2020. It shows cherry trees in bloom, something celebrated in Japan with outdoor parties which include family and friends but also a bittersweet sense of transience; Iwane includes figures from Japanese folklore too, suggesting a respect for nature and spirituality that photography, and the scientific worldview from which it emerged, tried to sideline. A New River is also underpinned by a very personal grief, because Iwane was under a blossoming cherry tree when she found out that her sister had died. Images of her sister also feature, in a moving projection of shots gathered after her death.

“It was a very hard time for me for a long time, and I kept thinking about her every day,” says Iwane, in a video made by Kyotographie. “Maybe after one or a couple of years, there was the day that I realised ‘Oh today I never thought about her’. So during the making of A New River, I recalled the day that I realised I forgot about her and I thought ‘Maybe I will forget about this strange time of the state of emergency’, and about how easily people can forget about things. So then I started to search for photographs that I have taken of my sister and my family, because I won’t be able to photograph my sister or anyone who has passed but the picture and the memory stay.” 

Kyotographie festival is noted for its innovative approach to installation and the exhibition at Japan House is no exception; made with the help of spatial designer Hiromitsu Konishi, it includes the circle as a motif. A round table gathers Kawada’s publications in a room devoted to his The Last Cosmology, for example, which features celestial phenomena such as eclipses. In Iwane’s show, the panoramic shots snake through the gallery, while images from A New River hang in concentric waves round the visitor.

Throughout, the exhibition is darkly-lit, spotlights picking out the photographs; the viewer’s first-hand reality is thrown into shadow and the world of the images surfaces, but this is less photography as observation, and more evocation of emotion.

item.title: Jip Schalkx on social media, self-branding and our hybrid social reality - 1854 Photography
item.description:
© Jip Shalkx

The winner of the People’s Choice Award in this year’s Female in Focus talks through her work and how we can navigate a world where the physical and digital are increasingly intertwined

We have all experienced it: that heart-sinking moment when you look around the dinner table and realise that every person is glued to their device. “You’re together, but not together. And you’re all friends, so you’re probably all consuming the same content,” says Dutch photographer Jip Schalkx. She describes this as a “hybrid social reality” – a blended state of existence where our physical and digital worlds are increasingly intertwined.

The contradiction of this new reality, of creating an illusion of togetherness while actually promoting isolation, is what inspired the 28-year-old artist’s award-winning image, 4ever &ver &ver. In it Schalkx depicts six girls lying together peacefully, headphones on. The scene resonates instantly, offering a gentle critique on the impact of technology on our social and emotional worlds.

The image is a poignant commentary on one of the most defining issues of our times, and for that it has been awarded the People’s Choice Award in this year’s Female in Focus prize, curated around the theme ‘On the Cusp’. The annual prize for women photographers is organised by British Journal of Photography and sponsored by Nikon. “The photograph powerfully reflects how young people navigate a world where visibility and the pressures of social media increasingly shape everyday intimacy,” says Ruby Nicholson, senior communications manager for Nikon Northern Europe. “It beautifully captures the delicate balance between connection and isolation, making it a resonant and highly relevant image for our times.”

Shalkx reveals that the image belongs to a video piece, in which the girls sleep to a looping soundscape stitched out of audio grabs from social media. It includes clips from protests for Palestine, beauty influencers advocating for “vampire sleep” on TikTok, and Kylie Jenner’s viral “realising stuff” statement. It mimics the “forever loop” of scrolling, and the muddled lines between our physical and digital realities.

This video is part of a wider body of work investigating “how algorithmic modification influences how young people communicate in this capitalistic world”. For Shalkx, the questions began to emerge during an internship in Barcelona, after which she returned to the Netherlands and felt a jarring sense of alienation. “There’s this work-driven force,” she says, comparing the social codes of her home country to a city like Barcelona, which is noticeably laidback. She considers the Netherlands among the most capitalistic in the world, and “when I got back, I noticed it a lot more. I felt alienated, and I didn’t understand why”.

“The algorithm sees me. It knows what I want, before I even know myself” – Jip Shalx

About How You Sell Yourself. Shalkx argues that in a world of hyper-capitalism and constant self-optimisation, the boundaries between our real personalities and our branded selves have collapsed. It is true, because the algorithm dictates who is seen and valued, and that requires us to sell ourselves in a very specific way. In drawing heavily on Guy Debord’s ideas of capitalism and image-consumption in The Society of the Spectacle, Shalkx argues that this has redefined how young adults in the Netherlands live their lives – what they choose to wear, how they talk to one another, what they eat, and how they behave.

Writing on this subject was all well and good, but translating these thoughts into images was a whole other challenge. Shalkx’s process combines deep research and constant observation – looking at people, but also Tumblr, Pinterest, books and magazines. It was through this process that the image at the centre of 4ever &ver &ver first appeared:“I saw it so vividly in my head, of the girls lying next to each other.” Her instinct, as a photography student, was to shoot a still image, until a friend suggested she film it instead. Filming, it turned out, gave the piece something a photograph could not: “That kind of friction, where it’s almost still, like they’re in ‘sleep mode’.”

Two more video pieces followed. The second features a dance sequence, choreographed by Ūla Naujokaitytė, and based on TikTok-style movements. “It’s about how language changes, and how social media has changed how we behave with our bodies,” Schalkx says. The idea came after seeing a group of teenagers communicating using TikTok-coded gestures. She staged the dance in front of a typical Dutch house, but with an ominous factory smoking behind it, deliberately slowing the choreography to subvert TikTok’s usual sharp, snappy energy and create a movement that is far from appealing “in the algorithmic sense”.

The third video takes a more satirical turn, and stars her friend Victor. “I’m part of something bigger here,” he says, professing his love for social media in a one-take monologue shot at a bus stop. “The algorithm sees me. It knows what I want, before I even know myself.” Shalkx wrote the script using AI, she says, prompting it with themes from her long-running conversations with Victor about social media. Alongside the three videos sits Cloud9, a series of mirror portraits printed on glass. This work investigates the tension between the digital and physical self: who are we, Schalkx asks, the version of ourselves we perform online, or the version that exists in real life?

All of this is in part informed by Shalkx’s own conflicted relationship with the internet. She grew up mostly without a smartphone, and remembers social media’s arrival. “I come from the Tumblr era,” she says. “I loved that you could aestheticise things, like what you’d do with a magazine. Cutting things out and putting them on a mood board.” But the internet soon outgrew its innocence. “Back then there were no ads. It was just people posting stuff. Then it became more and more commercialised,” she says. “Enterprise culture became the norm.” It is a shift the writer Cory Doctorow has termed “enshittification”: the slow decay of once-useful platforms as they are optimised for profit. 

These days, Schalkx’s own presence online is more guarded. “I love my images, but right now I’m taking a step back,” she says. Yet the same questions continue to occupy her practice, and her next body of work takes it a step further in a deeper exploration of self-branding and commodification. 

“A lot of people are doing projects about the internet, and a lot of it adopts a very specific aesthetic,” Schalkx says, referring to glitchy collages, work that uses AI, or 3D rendered elements. “I never really resonated with this way of talking about it. It feels scary.” Rather than depicting the darkness literally, Shalkx wants to speak about the subject in a more human, recognisable way. “Making people scared – I don’t think that’s the only way we can communicate about it.”

Shalkx is right, because we have experienced these conversations too; long discussions about the ills of the internet that end with a collective sigh of doom. Schalkx’s work asks many questions, and while there is never an easy answer, the proposition of recognition rather than fear is a strong one. And maybe that recognition is the first step to finding a way back to each other.

Female in Focus is at International Centre for the Image until 25 October 2026

item.title: Among people with Jillian Edelstein - 1854 Photography
item.description:
President Nelson Mandela, Tuynhuys, the Presidential house. From the series Truth and Lies, 1996-2001 © Jillian Edelstein

Now extended until the end of October, Jillian Edelstein’s retrospective at Stills Gallery, Edinburgh shows her deep engagement with people, from those at South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation to swimmers at Hampstead Heath

Born in Cape Town, Jillian Edelstein is best-known for her work on South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Photographing perpetrators, victims, and other individuals involved in the public hearings which grappled with the country’s Apartheid history from 1996-2002 – and some of the landscapes involved – Edelstein worked on the project for four years. When she published it as a book in 2002, Truth and Lies included endorsements from Archbishop Desmond Tutu, Gillian Slovo and Pumla Gobodo-Madikizela (Research Chair in Studies in Historical Trauma and Transformation at Stellenbosch University in South Africa), plus extensive text and reflections written by Edelstein. 

But though Truth and Lies is important, it’s also not the only thing Edelstein has made. In fact when she made it she wasn’t living in South Africa any more; she has now been a UK resident for much longer than she lived in Africa. Edelstein’s retrospective at Stills Gallery includes Truth and Lies, but it also includes other projects from across her five decades of work. Curated by Tracey Marshall-Grant, it’s titled Jillian Edelstein – Among People to mark the photographer’s commitment to individuals from many different communities, and includes early images from Johannesburg and Cape Town, and from an anthropological project in Portugal, right up to recent work from 2020-22, showing the community of swimmers who use Hampstead Heath’s ponds. 

“People are people and you can learn from everyone. I try to treat everyone with equality.” Jillian Edelstein

It also includes images from Edelstein’s long-running portrait series Affinities, which explores creative partnerships; her long term project on the Sangoma, traditional healers on the Lesotho-South African border; and portraits taken from Ukraine, from her book Here and There: An Expedition of Sorts, published by GOST in 2024. Edelstein has also made work about male suicide, migration, the West Bank, and poverty in the UK, and has shot portraits for publications such as The New York Times Magazine, The FT Weekend Magazine, Vogue, GQ, and Esquire. The National Portrait Gallery holds more than 100 of her prints. 

She has shot people from wildly different communities and walks of life, in fact, from those immersed in wealth to those facing very hard times. “It’s a privilege, because people are people and you can learn from everyone,” says Edelstein. “I try to treat everyone with equality, I think that can show something really powerful…In South Africa I remember thinking how fascinating it was that the perpetrators put themselves forward to be captured, in a vain kind of way. That was very striking. I think there is quantifiable experience, and you have to face that and think how to portray it.”

Born in 1958, Edelstein originally studied social work rather than photography; her first job was at the National Institute for the Crime and Rehabilitation of Offenders in Cape Town, where she worked with mainly men who were in prison, or had recently been released. There was energy and compassion in this work, but she had discovered photography at university and soon decided that shooting documentary and portrait images was a way to continue social work “without having to write out the case report”, she says.

Working as an assistant during the week, which allowed her to learn technical skills as well as how to use lights and print, she started to work as a press photographer at a time of great unrest in South Africa, as people struggled to overthrow Apartheid. Eventually she became a photojournalist, working for The Rand Daily Mail in 1982–83, and The Star newspaper in 1984. She worked alongside Black colleagues and was well aware of her privilege compared to them, she says; she was able to take greater risks as a White, “because the costs for them would have been so much higher, they had to keep in line”. 

Edelstein won awards for her work but in 1985 decided to leave to formally study documentary photography at the London College of Printing [now the London College of Communication]. She lasted six months before Michael Cranmer, then-picture editor of The Sunday Times, came to do a guest lecture and saw some of her work. “He said ‘What are you doing here?!’” Edelstein laughs. “He gave me a commission and then Andrew Neil [then-editor of The Sunday Times] saw the portrait and said ‘Offer her a contract’. It was sort of extraordinary even then.”

Edelstein says she is grateful to have been a press photographer then though, when staff jobs did exist and commissions were more generous; she could support herself with this work, and the commissions also helped her access to hard-to-reach individuals. Many of her personal projects include commissioned elements, such as the portrait of Nelson Mandela in Truth and Lies, or the comedians French and Saunders in Affinities.

But her success also wasn’t just down to luck or the structures of the day; working in an extremely male-dominated environment – and as a single mother – she still tried to leverage her work to help others. In fact she’s acutely aware of power, and how it’s unfairly brought to bear. “Looking back across these photographs, I’m struck by how much my work has been shaped by my early engagements or interactions with inequality and subjugation,” she states in Stills’ press material, “one asserting an unjust superiority over another”.

She tells me that her training in social work, anthropology, psychology and sociology helped her refine these insights; she thinks about power at both a macro and micro level, in terms of the interpersonal and the societal. There’s the delicate balance between directing a shoot and giving her subjects space, for example, but then there’s also authority and how it plays out. She tells me an anecdote about photographing five members of the security police in South Africa, for example, who were testifying before the Truth Commission for the murder of one of their Black colleagues, who they had decided was informing on them to the ANC; it was a difficult, intimidating shoot but a few days later she saw one of the men on his own in the airport, lacking all the bravado of his strength-in-numbers. 

Edelstein is also well-attuned to the role of photography and observation, however, the negative ways in which the gaze can be used, and she can therefore be implicated. In Truth and Lies she writes about the bright lights which illuminated the townships in the 1970s and 80s, the ‘eye of the state’ which kept residents under surveillance. In the West Bank she noted something similar in the turnstiles, she says, which allows Israeli soldiers to control peoples’ movements. “This practical handiwork that autocratic governments put in place, it operates and it’s horrifying,” she says.

Edelstein is also saddened by the current state of the world, the fact that terrible things happen and that “no matter how present the camera is, it hasn’t stopped them”. Even so, she’s still enthusiastic about her current work, which includes a commission photographing women who have survived sexual violence and abuse. “It’s the challenge of photographing someone, the dance that you have to do,” she says. “What you give is what you get back.” Then she smiles and asks me about myself.
